FLuvrs are like fiddles—no good without beaux. THE shortness of life is very often owing to the irregularities of the liver. "I hate to hear people talk behind one's back," as the robber said when the constable cried out "Stop thief ?" A PATIENT should pay his doctor as soon as he gets well, just to show there is no ill-feeling. IT is all very well to talk about rising in the world. Can you rise early in the morning? SPEECH may be silver; but there is lot 9of it that is not sterling. "So far, so good," as the boy said when he had finished the first pot of his mother's jam. IF the old proverb "Care killed a cat" is true, then when a man goes cat-hunting, he should take care.

DUNN : "Why is it that you never have any money the day after you receive your salary?" be Fassett : "Its all owing to other people." TILE woman wi.o is vain of her beauty is as wise as the man who is vain of his brains. _

Loss OF SIGHT AND SPEECH—The captain of a trading vessel, having some contraband goods on board which he wished to land, said to an excise- man whom lie knew, "If I was to put a half- t:rown-picee upon each of your eyes, could you gee 1" The answer was, " No ; and if I had another in my mouth I could not spyak." _

"THERE s one curious thing about discovering places," said Johnny, after he got through with his study. " Take Bermuda, for instance. It was discovered by a man named Bermudes. How he ,happened to stumble on a place with a name just like -111 s beats me."

THE BEST APPLES. —Two boys, seut into the country by a "fresh-air-fund," thus conversed: "Say, Pat, will we see apples on trees?" "Ow course you said his companion, with a tone of conscious superiority. "But I don't like them," added he. "I ate some in the counthry last summer, an' they were sour. Apples that grow in barels is best."

IN THE THIIMES. —An Envious Contemporary (to Miss Bud long) : "And so you are really engaged to Mr. Timid Smitlik ins?" Miss Budlong (quite provokingly) : "Yes, dear; and I want you to suggest something sweet and tender to go in my engagement ring." Ervious Contemporary "if I were in your place, Id just have the simple word 4 Eureka.' "

IN GOOD Humouu.—Pat has a great power of enjoyment, after all, and always laughs at the right time. One day he saw a ball attack a man, and he had to hold on to his sides with both hands, the scene was so funny. After a little the animal turned his attention in another direction, and poor Pat, after exploring the heights, came down with a thump on lie other side of the fence. Ile rubbed his wounds,,and as he trudged along, the worse for wear, he said to liiineif, " Faith, Pm glad I had my laugh when I did, or I wouldn't ha,c had it at all, at all." CARVING AND GILDING. A splendidly - gilt dining-room, with almost nothing on the table to eat, was the peculiarity of a Boston miser. A wag was invited to dinner on a certain occasion, and the host asked him if he didn't think the room elegant. "Yes," was the reply ; " but it is not quite according to my taste." "And pray what change would you make ?" asked the host. " he answered, "if this were my house, you, know, I would have (looking at the ceiling) less gilding (and he glanced furtively at the dining table) and more carving !" VERY POLITE. —At the ball Ferguson has just conducted his partner baek to her place; but, instead of retiring after the usual compliments, he plants himself in front of her with an air of con- siderable embarrassment. "Is there anything that you desire, sir ?" asked the lady, noticing his uneasiness. "No, miss—that is—l mean, my crush hat, which has had the honour of finding itself actually—upon the same chair as yourself." Goon EVIDENCE. —" Do you think Charlie really loves me, mamma ?" asked the fair young girl anxiously. "Certainly he does. Haven't you noticed that he always wears the gloves you bought him for a Christmas present, though they are two sizes too large ?" LITERARY CRITICISM. O'Connel, meeting a literary friend one day, exclaimed : "I have just seen a capital thing in your last new pamphlet." "Did you eagerly replied the delighted listener. "What was it ?" "A pound of butter," was the merciless answer."

NOT FASTIDIOUS. —A tramp rapped at the door the other day, and asked the woman if she could spare him a piece of bread. "No, I can't," replied the woman. "And if you knew who I was you wouldn't have come here." "Oh, and who are you?" asked the tramp. "I am a policeman's wife, and if he was in he would take you." "That's true," replied the tramp ; "for if he'd take you he' take anybody." AN AWKWARD JUG. —Lady "You don't mean to tell me, Mary, that my new crystal milk-jug is bro— !" div.head: "CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

It was once my fortune to accompany a body pf Conservative working men to Hatfield, where they wandered about LGrd Salisbury's grounds, went through some of the rooms of his mansion, dined in his riding school in the afterr.oon, and listened to speeches from his Lordship, who occupied the chair, and from a well known and energetic Tory who is now deceased, Mr. James Anderson Rose. To me it was a wonderful •sight, but I assumed that the working men were of a class that had never thought for a moment about politics, and knew little of the standing historical cleavage between Liberalism and Toryism. But on the way home I had a long and interesting conversation with the leader who marshalled the little army during its day's outing. And a Radical he certainly was when I had fairly penetrated his con- fidence. There was not a shred of Toryism about him. Yet he had drunk Lord Salisbury's beer, dined off his joints, and cheered his speeches, and had eat like an accredited incarnation of Toryism with other honoured guests at the head of the table. I find that he was really opposed to the aristocracy of the House of Lords; he was opposed to the Establishment ; he wanted a wider franchise so that the democracy would be strengthened and have full scope. I did not say" Oh, hypocrite," but I asked him how many more of his band were of the ; same opinion, and he confessed it was the political creed of nearly the whole.

The announcement that an official intimation of the retirement of the Duke of Cambridge from the I office of Commander-in-Chief in March next may soon be expected will be welcome to more than I Army reformers. It is rather premature, however, to fix upon Lord Wolseley as virtually his successor in the reorganised Horse Guards, under the new name, of chief of the staff. But if the post of honour falls to Lord Wolseley we shall at least have ' a general at the head of the army, and not a mere commander of a division who once saw a little ser- vice during the Crimean War, but who otherwise is quite inexperienced in commanding an army or conducting a campaign. His appointment to his present office did great injustice to men vastly his superiors in experience, in standing, and in the art of war; and, unfortunately, the country is not yet out of the ruts in which similar injustice might be perpetrated. It will have an opportunity of testing this when the new official chief of the army is ap- pointed. There have been so many disappointments in connection with the extradition of Jabez Balfour that one hesitated on ;Sunday to credit the telegram that he had been at last handed over to the English detective who has so long been waiting for him at Buenos Ayres. The confirmation of the news by the Home Office puts the matter beyond doubt, and when this interesting figure appears before an English judge and jury it will be a moment of genuine exwltation to all who have been brought to ruin by the gigantic frauds with which his name is associated. The whole secret history of the Libera- tor Society will now be disclosed; and possibly not a few whose heads are held high will begin to tremble at the exposure from which they have I hitherto escaped.

I learn that the War Office regards with consider- able sympathy a formal suggestion which the Duke of Connaught has made that 10,000 volunteers should spend a week together at Aldershot at intervals during the year. In this way, the Duke argues, he could give the volunteer force a general comprehension of the principles which govern mobilisation schemes. The Duke would have the volunteers carefully drilled beforehand, so that they could at once start the week's work with tactical exercises and field movements, and thus make the very best use of the time available. This would necessitate a careful preparatory instruction of field officers, on the necessity of which the Duke dwells with considerable emphasis.

At the Imperial Institute on Tuesday a large Party sat down to eat Queensland beef and New Zealand lamb, and both were thoroughly enjoyed. The trade in beef from Queensland is of great im- portance to that colony. Queensland started its productive life with the cultivation of sugar, but the sugar bounties seem to have nearly killed that industry. So now Queensland is anxious to com- pete with other countries in the supply of meat to England. It was stated at the luncheon that Eng- land produces 68 per cent, of the meat required by its population, and that the Australian colonies, excluding New Zealand. scarcely exports 1 per cent. of the 32 per cent. deficiency. There are seven millions of cattle in Queensland, and there seems to be no valid reason why an important trade should not be developed not only in England but also in other European countries where agriculture does not keep pace with the increasing population. Recently some Queensland beet was sent to Vienna, where the Town Council appointed a committee to examine it and report. The chief :'lealth officer gave it as his opinion that it was equal to any fresh-killed beef in Germany.

. I obtained some remarkable figures as to the pro- vision made for the guests at the Guildhall bauqUet on Friday. I should explain that everything is done on a rather liberal scale, because it is a point of honour with successive Lord Mayor and Sheriffs —who combined bear the cost—that there should be an abundant supply for the poor of the city left over. There have been 24 turtles specially imported from the West Indies, made into 100 gallons of soup; 4,000 oysters will be opened by twenty men ; there will be 500 lobsters, 200 large soles, 120 tur- keys, 200 partridges, 100 pheasants, 300 plovers,2oo capons, 20 barns, GOO cutlets, 200 veal and ham pies; 160 pairs of sweetbreads, 200 calves' feet for jelly, and 1,200 portions of sweets and ices provided. The guests will number 900. Beyond the ordinary Idishes, the usual two huge barons of beef will furnish one of the courses. It is thus that the City maintains its'usefulness.

The story current within the last few days that Mr. John Morley is likely to offer the commissioner - ship of education to Mr. Sexton is a rather old tale. It was in circulation in the House of Commons before the termination of last session, but was not credited by any but opponents of the Government, and by not many of them. It was not the virtue of the Government that induced this disbelief, but the well-known fact that the Irish members are under a mutual bond not to accept any office of emolument, from either a Tory or a Liberal Government. The commissionership was not then vacant, but it is vacant now, and the story which connects Mr. Sexton's. name with it has been now revived. But if Mr. Sexton were to accept the office, the salary of which i 3 £1,500 a year, it would ruin himself and the section of the Irish party to which he belongs, unless indeed, that section were held to- gether by the action and by the influence of the priests over their flecks. The anti-Parneilite party in the House, who have almost fallen to pieces al- ready, would inevitably break up, and Mr. Redmond and his eight followers would stump every consti- tuency in Ireland to make it known that the actual chief, though not nominally the chief of the anti- Parnellites had sold himself to the English Govern- ment. Mr. Morley's position in the matter of IEI6II education is a very difficult one, and it would not be made smoother by the appointment of Mr. Sexton, which would in all probability seriously affect the policy of the National Board. It would not upset the Irish alliance, but it would cost the Government at the election a good many Irish seats. --- Both political parties are now entering upon the most energetic preparations for the general e:ection which each of them feels might be sprung upon the country sooner than either expects. It is generally stated that the Liberals are behind in the selection and allocation of candidates, and, though the fact cannot be quite accurately known by anybody except those at headquatlers, there would seem to be some substratum of truth in the allegation. The Conservatives are equally busy. So far as the Ministerialists are concerned, the prepatations do not as yet imply any abandonment of the intention to proceed with the ramaining items of the New- castle programme, in the coming session, but the work and programme of the Ministry have now reached a stage when all sorts of parliament con- tingences might arise without a moment's warning. Though the Government has made up its mind to go on with legislation next session, it is by no means certain t tat it will be prudent to do so, as the arguments are quite as heavy against such a course as for

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY NOVEMBER 10,1894.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY NOVEMBER 10,1894.
LADIES' LETTER

Mary Elizabeth Kyel, a London lady, who passed the century mark four years ago, has slept twenty thousand nights und-r one roof. The wife of the Italian Prime Minister, Crispi, is an ardent lover of cigarettes, and enjoys puffing a cloud whenever she is disengaged. It is not generally known, says the "Princess," that when the Princess of Wales travels two indispensable adjuncts in her impedimenta are a favourite white cat and a table lull of ordinary aed assorted little china animals, such as can be bought in any toy shop or bazaar. These entail no little trouble upon her atten- dants as she will never allow her rooms to be dis- mantled until the last moment. The packing of these fragile pets has been the cause of the losing of more than one train, and a good deal of irritation on the part of the Princess's immediate circle.

Mourning in Russia. Mourning in Russia is of a very pronounced kind. It destroys all beauty and almost all comfort. It lasts longer even than the deepest grief-period in England. Coarse, heavy, woollen materials, disagreeable to the touch and unresponsive to the light, are made in shapes that denote nothing of the figure they shroud. The idea is to express complete indifference to everything but grief for the departed,and this is carried out in every detail of the costume, which is almost disfiguring in its obtrusive lack of elegance. Even a careful coiffure was once considered inconsistent with the attitude of the mourner, but among the higher classes this exaggera- tion of the expression of woe has of late succumbed t) to common sense. English crape is invariably used by all Continental nations in their mourning, this being a manufacture in which this country enjoys an undisputed pre-eminence.
THE DOUBLE LIFE:
OR, THE HAMPTON MYSTERY. By the Author of "DARKWOOD."
CHAPTER XL. A GREAT JOY. i cannot speak, tears so obstruct my words And choke me with unutterable joy. OTWAY.

It was the figure of poor little Fay. He looked pale and thin, and the vestiges of a great sorrow were visible under the excitement kindling his features. He had heard Giralda's voice, and, despite the command of Peggy Willsey to remain hidden un- til after the departure of her guests, he had yen- tured from his concealment, a great hope springing up within him that his parents and Giralda had conic for him.

_ At sight of Giralda his joy flashed up into his violet eyes, and reddened his cheeks, and over- flowed in his boyish soul. With a great cry, he sprang forward, calling her name. With an answering cry, Giralda met him half way, and caught him to her breast. "Oh, my darling! my darling 1" she murmured, laughing and crying in a breath. "Oh, Fay! My poor little brother 1 " She sank down on the lounge, weak and power- less, the boy clinging to her, and begging to be taken to his mother.

"You shall go to mamma, Fay," she said, showering kisses upon him. "You are quite safe now. I shall not lose sight of you until I place you in mamma's arms." She clasped the little fellow closer, and looked over his golden head with a defiant glance at Peggy Willsey, who was regarding the couple in a sort of stupefaction. "He is my brother !" explained Giralda. "Lord Adlowe stole him from our home, in order to have a hold upon us. No one shall take him from me." "Not while Dorothy Pumpton lives 1" cried the Park housekeeper, comprehending the situation, and facing Peggy with a warlike mien. "I will protect those two poor children with my life 1" Peggy stared at her visitors, as if fancying that they were losing their senses. The attitude of Fay, however, assured her that he shared the general delusion, if delusion there was. "I can't understand all this," she muttered. -4' "It's as plain as the nose on your face, Peggy, Willsey, or as your face itself, for that matter, responded Mrs. Pumpton, sharply. "Lord Ad- lowe stole the young gentleman from his home. And you, it seems, are his accomplice—" "No, Mrs. Pumpton, no!' interrupted the shepherdess indignantly. "Mr. Wigby, my lord's valet, brought the little lad here, and told me that he was Lord Adlowe's ward, and that his health was delicate, and his mind not quite right, on account of a late fever, and that I must keep him close to prevent his losing himself on the Downs. I believed Mr. Wigby. Ask the young gentleman if I haven't treated him well, poor little dear 1" "Yes, she has," protested Fay, earnestly, lifting his head from his sister's breast. "She has been good to me, and told me stories, and let me count the sheep, and given me a ride every day on the funniest little donkey you ever saw. But this isn't home !" and his lip quivered. "And though she's kind, she aint my own folks, you know. I wanted papa and mamma. and Giralda. and Rup- ert."
"Bless his little heart !" said Mrs. Pumpton wiping her eyes. "Lie is Mr. Geoffrey's own son that he is !" _ _

"Mr; Geoffrey's son ! " repeated Peggy, her honest face working with emotion. "I wish I had known it; But it isn't too late yet. Miss Tre- velyan," and she turned to Giralda, "Lord Adlowe might have found a worse keeper for the little lad than me. You heard the young gentleman say that I had trelted him well. You do not blame me for believing what I could not know to be false? "
"Did not Fay tell you who he was?" asked Giralda.

"Yes, Miss. He said his father was a Spanish count, and that his home was some everlasting place, I don't rightly remember the name, but I thought his mind wasn't right after the fever. You forgive me for my stupidity ? " "I have nothing to forgive," returned Giralda. "It is Lord Adlowe whom I blame. But I thank you, Peggy, for having been kind to the poor little fellow. And now," she added, "1 must get word to mamma at once that Fay is found, and safe. I must telegraph. What is the nearest station?" "Dalton—ten inUes from here," said Peggy. "But you can't go, Miss, until afternoon, for your horses are dead tired. You look tired out yourself, Miss. If you would lie down a while you would feel strong for your journey." Mrs. Pumpton echoed this counsel, and declared that she also needed rest, and would lie down an hour or two, if her young lady was will- ing. Thus pressed, Giralda acquiesced, although she was full of impatience to relieve the anxiety of Lady Beatrice in regard to Fay. Peggy invited the maiden into the inner room, and the invitation was accepted, Fay still clinging to his sister. This apartment was as neat as the other, white curtains being at the windows, a bright home-made carpet on the floor, and toilet appurtenances and a neat white bed holding prominent places against the walls.

"You can feel perfectly safe here," said the hostess. "Believe me, Miss, lam your true friend, as well as Master Fay's. If I had suspected the truth, I should have sent word to your mother, if I could have discovered her address. I would not harm a fly, Miss, much less knowingly aid such a villain as Lord Adlowe to injure poor Mr. Geoffrey." "I believe you, Peggy," said Giralda, with a look and a smile that w armed and comforted the woman's heart. "I thank you for your kindness to my brother, and papa will yet thank you." Peggy withdrew, and the brother and sister were left to themselves. Giralda listened to Fay's story, which began with his abduction from the Evergreens, and told him as much of what had since transpired as he could understand, or she deemed it best for him to know. And then, gathering him in her arms, she lay down on the bed and dropped asleep, a peace that was almost divine neAtling in her soul. It was afternoon when she awakened. Fay was sitting up at her aide, regarding her with grave inertness, as if fearing that she would vanish be- fore his eyes. The hum of voices came from the outer room. She started up at once, half expecting to find herself in her pleasant room at Trevelyan Park.

" Ah, little Fay," she said, caressing him. "It was Providence that guid€d me to you. I shall always remember now that there is a guiding hand in our sorrows as well as our joys." "When are we going home, Giralda?" asked Fay, gravely. "I told you, dear, that papa and Rupert were gone away, and that mamma is in London. We cannot go directly back to The Evergreens." "Then I am to go to your new home?" ques- tioned the boy. "I have no new home now, Fay. Trust me. I shall take you away from here directly, but where we are to find refuge I do not yet know." She arose and made her toilet, a task that was soon accomplished, and then, taking Fay, entered the outer room. The table was daintily laid for two persons' and a neat little dinner smoked on the hearth. Mrs. Pumpton and her hostess had dined, and were conversing confidentially before the fire. They both arose at Giralda's entrance, with many kindly inquiries, and Peggy hastened to set up the dinner. • It's only one o'clock, Miss," she said, glancing at the deal clock on a painted shelf. "The horses ore ready for your journey, if you must go on to Dalton to-day. I've a lad tending the sheep, and son guide you to Dalton, if you wish." Giralda accepted the proffer with gratitude and strong sensation of relief. She had been appre- hensive of difficulty in the continuation of her journey, suspecting that Mrs. Pumpton was as ignorant as herself of the route to Dalton. "I shall go direct to a telegraph station, and telegraph to mamma," she said, with her usual decision. "And then I will seek out lodgings for Fay and myself in some humble, quiet place, where we can remain undisturbed until I can hear from mamma. I shall be grateful to you, dear Mrs. Pumpton, if you will see me settled before going back to the Park." "I intend to," declared Mrs. Plimpton. "I shall not leave you, except in safe hands." "I know a family in Dalton, relations of mine," said Peggy, "where Miss Trevelyan would be safe. It's a quiet, humble place, but as good as this in every respect." " We will go there, then," said Giralda. Peggy withdrew to make a few final prepara- tions for departure, and Mrs. Pumpton waited upon the young guests. The dinner was soon over, and Giralda and Fay were then eager to set out. Zot tke_tinle the horses and donkey were brou2ht
from Wee stable, where they had been sheltered, the travellers were quite ready for their journey.

"Pay will ride with me," said Giralda, caressing her pretty mare, who arched her slender neck proudly under the maiden's gentle touch. "Zulime can carry us both." She mounted easily, and the Park housekeeper handed up Fay, whom Giralda pla.-:ed securely before her on the saddle. Mrs. Pumpton climbed into her saddle, and Peggy having locked her small cottage, mounted the donkey, and the little cavalcade set out.

The sun was shining, and a crisp breeze was 1 blowing over the wide Downs. The gorse, already I well-grown, was waving to and fro like a gentle sea. There was a slight chill in the atmosphere, making motion pleasant. Flocks of sheep were , seen gazing lazily, or moving about under the superintendence of a shepherd lad, to whom Peggy I gave a few final directions as she rode past. 4 Those sheep are all mine," she observed, with ; proud satisfaction, glancing at her possessions.. "I known every one of them, I believe. I am almost too rich, I sometimes think, for a lone woman. There's nothing weighs one down like riches, when one can't use it all, and have no one to share it with you," and she sighed. "Why don't you sell out, Peggy, and move into a town ? " asked the Park housekeeper. "It must be lonely living here!" "It is sometimes. But I won't sell out," said Peggy, "until I know more about George—Neg- wyn, you know. He may come home from Aus- tralia yet, if he went there' as some say, poor and. discouraged. It would be a nice thing for him to step Into such a, home and such riches, wouldn't It ? "
"You don't mean that you'd marry him, if he clime back unmarried ?" questioned Mrs. Pumpton, shocked. "And that you'd make him master of all you own ? "

''Why not," asked Peggy, simply, "if he lotres me yet? If I could have him with me, I am sure I have influence enough over him to make a man of him. No matter how he comes back, if he isn't married, and if a spark of his old love for me re- mains, I will receive him kindly." Giralda's face expressed her sympathy with this resolve.

"What is that dark object yonder ?" asked Fay, pointing to the north of their route. Giralda looked, perceiving a dark mass whose outlines she could not fairly distinguish in the glare of the sun. She called the attention of her corn panions to it. Peggy halted and gazed at the object, shading her eyes with her hand. "It's a horse that has fallen after leaping the fissure behind it," she exclaimed exciredly. "There seems to be a man half under the horse 1"

She urged her donkey towards the object, Giralda dashing past her on her mare. The maiden was the first to reach the scene, and the sight that met her gaze made her sick with horror. A ravine or fissure where once a stream had flowed, crossed the DGwns in this place like a deep furrow. Its bed and walls were clothed with deep furze. By the very edge of the ravine a horse lay dead. In leaping the fissure it had broken one of its legs as it seemed, and also re- ceived some internal injury. Half under the horse pinned to the earth by the animal's body a man was lying. His face was turned downward, and his hands were clenched as In agony. Giralda leaped to the ground and clasped his wrists, feeling his pulse, and then laid her hand on his heart.

"He is not dead," she cried. "He is simply unconscious. If we could only free him from this crushing weight.' By this time Mrs. Pumpton and Peggy had reached the scene. They hastily dismounted, and advanced to aid Giralda.
Peggy's quick eyes speedily took in the situa- tion.

"I think that we can get the man out with the aid of the shepherd lad," said she, motioning her assistant to approach. The lad came up at full speed, and the process of rescuing the insensible man was at once inaugu- rated. The young shepherd and Peggy, who had a man's strength, undertook to raise that portion of the fallen steed which pinioned the unfortunate horseman, while Mrs. Pumpton and Giralda, who was all activity and excitement, undertook, at the eventful moment, to draw out the prostrate figure. It was a hard task, but it was well accom- plished. The man was drawn to a place of safety, and his face was turned up to the sunlight. As her gaze rested upon the dark and unprepos- sessing features, Giralda uttered a cry of surprise. "It is Haskins, Lord Adlowe's man ! ' she exclaimed. "He must have been going to your house, Peggy!" Peggy did not answer. She was bending over the unfortunate man, a strangely yearning look on her face, a strangely wistful look in her eyes. Suddenly her face glowed with recognition, and she fell on her knees, sobbing: "It is George! It is George! Come back to me at last, after all these years.'

She put her arms around him, lifting his head to her knees, chafing his hands, and calling on him hysterically to look up and know her. " Negwyn ?" ejaculated Giralda, almost reeling. That is Negwyn ?" "She is right. It is Negwyn I" exclaimed the Park housekeeper. "How blind I have been! It takes love to make people sharp-sighted." "That Negwyn !' murmured Giralda an agony of regret sweeping over her soul. "If I had only known of it before! If I only had penetrated his disguise! It may not be toa late yet. He is not dead." She dispatched the shepherd lad for water, and when it was brought, helped Peggy to bathe the pallid face and lifeless hands, despite the remon- strances of Mrs. Pumpton. Her exertions were soon crowned with suc- cess. Haskins, or Negwyn, as we will hereafter call him, stirred himself feebly, and opened his eyes. "George 1" cried the faithful woman, who had waited for him so long, " George ! do you know me?" No look of recognition came into the hollow eyes of the injured man. He moaned faintly, and muttered an incoherent sentence. Giralda again felt his pulse. It was quick and bounding. "The accident must have happened hours since," she said, anxiously. "His injury and Cu _

- . i - - exposure have thrown lum into a fever. kle must be got into the house and into a bed immedi- ately." "We can take him in. The way is not far," said Peggy, lifting a face glowing with joy, de- spite its anxiety. "Jamie, you and I can lift Mm."

MN arose to her feet, moving as gently as if the man had been a sleeping infant. Mrs. Pompton and the young shepherd hastened to lend their aid, and Negwyn was slowly carried towards the cottage. Giralda followed, leading the horses. By the time that Negwyn was got to bed he was In a raving fever. Mrs. Pumnton. who was skilled In eases oi sickness, shook her head gravely, am told Giralda privately that the man could not re- cover, and that she thought he would never at- tain command of his senses. _ _ _
"He must have a doctor at once," said the maiden. "Is there none to be found nearer than Dalton?"

Peggy shook her head. "Then let the shepherd guide us, and we will go on our way," said Giralda. "I will send the best doctor to be had. He will live—he must live to do justice to my poor wtonged father, and to make amends for your years of loneliness, Peggy 1 Oh, he must not die 1"

She lingered but a few moments by Negwyn's bedside, and then, her soul surging between hopes and sears—between a great joy and a great anxiety —she went out, mounted behind Fay, and a moment later was riding swiftly over the Burnt Down,, in company with Mrs. Pumpton and the shepbard guide. (To be continued).

div.head: MT DISAB.EST NELLIE,
div.p: MT DISAB.EST NELLIE,

The fashionable colours for millinery are per. venche and bright cherry. The first•named, whioh is neither blue nor purple, but a combination of the two, is being most extensively patronised in Paris, not only for hats and bonnets, but for gowns and mantles. It is by no means becoming to all, only suiting young, frenh complexions; but that is a mere matter of detail. All wear it—young and old—regardless of its individual suitability. Cherry (cerise), on the contrary, can he very generally worn; and wistaria, also a favourite shade, is well fitted, with its delicate lilac tones, to the matronly and elderly. Felt is the material most employed by milliners, and long jet buckles have superseded those of paste. Thick embroideries in gold, steel, multi-coloured beading, and jet forms the crowns of the Dutch shapes still a great deal worn. Oriental and Russian heavy emoroideries are also greatly affected. Another form of the Puritan shape has a rather fluted crown, and is covered with the new s'aade of sweet-pea pink in miroir velvet; a jet coronet surrounds the brim, and jet ornaments are sets amidst the handsome creamy guipure lace, which is the principal trimming; the strings are of black velvet. Bonnets promise to be larger than they have been for some time, which Is certainly a desirable thing, since the recent shapes have been more for ornament than use. They are, for the most part, close-fitting, and when for street wear have, in most cases, strings from an Inch to an inch and a-half wide.

Those who do their own dressmaking bave no doubt often realised the trouble and difficulty of properly fitting a bodice. The following sug- gestions may be of some interest to amateur dress- makers :—Take an old bodice which fits well; button it down the front, sewing the button-holes fast to the underpieoe, so that they cannot drag, and out the buttons off. Then take a piece of cardboard the size of the neck, and sew it in as a cover, and upon this raise a pincushion by means of raga and sawdust or bran. The sleeves mast be out off at the elbow, and tightly tied or sewn. Turn the figure up, and fill it tightly with bran or sawdust. Allow this to settle for two days, and then again pinch it and pound it until every crevice is tight and firm. Cut another piece of

cardboard to fill the bottom orifice, sew this well in, and cover the whole figura with muslin to pre- vent the bran coming out, and to give a good pin- hold. The model is now the exact shape of the Individual for whom the dress is intended, and only requires to be placed on the table to fit the material over. When the model becomes " flabby " it can be tightened by forcing the saw- dust or bran out of the arms into the body, and refilling the arms with fresh bran. A stylish dressing jacket might be made of pink and white striped flannel, or indeed of any other material; the turnover collar is feather-stitched with silk and eked with embroidered frills.

For boys the tight breeches and blouse shirt, slightly overhanging the waistband, is still the suit which finds most favour in the eyes of fashionable mothers; but a blouse, which has some novelty about it, is of velvete3n, and opens down the front In a V-shapi, to show a lawn or silk undershirt that ha 3 a large square collar, which is worn out- side the velveteen blouse. Thin flannel might be substituted for silk or lawn when the weather is severe. Ai to overcoats, the long, semi-fitting shape, witu one, two or three capes, gauntlet cuffs, and flap pockets, is very smart- looking for boys be- tween the ages of five and eight, while for older lads nothing seems 80 popular as the covert coat, In drab or tan•faced cloth, with strapped seams and velvet collar. An excellent coat for a girl of ten or twelve is of dark smoked-blue covert coating, trimmed with curucule rave/ s. With it looks well a black felt hat with rosette of pale blue velvet and black tips.

div.head: Men Who Wear Bracelets.
div.p: Men Who Wear Bracelets.

"It appears rather a large band to go round a woman's wrist! Well, it would be rather large if it were intended for a woman, but, as it happens, that is for a man," explained a fashionable jeweller not long since, in response to a remark of astonishment ex- pressed by the writer. "Oh, you need not look sur- prised, sir. There's nothing extraordinary in that. Go into the West-end clubs, and you'll see a score of men with wrists adorned with a thin gold or 'silver bangle. What do they wear them for? Well, for ornament. I suppose, most of them, but in three or four cases that have come under my notice it's a little bit of sentiment. The first time I ever made a bracelet for a man was about five or six years back, when a young fellow came into my place and asked me to measure his wrist. 'Make a note of the size,' said he, and you'll hear about it later on.' Two days afterwards a young lady drove up in a carriage, and ordered a plain gold bangle the size of the gentleman's wrist, at the same time leaving the measurement of her own. Next day back came the gentleman, ordered a similar brace- let for the lady, to be ready in a week, and both to be engraved on the inside with, 'As this band,golden and without end.' On the day appointed, the gentleman and lady called, the bracelets were fitted on, and the ends hammered together so as to form each, an endless circle. They paid me well for the job, and I never saw them afterwards, but I heard subsequently that the gentleman was an officer in a regiment ordered out to Egypt, and I suppose this little device was in token of their undying affection for each other. Another strange customer for a bracelet was a wealthy sportsman, well known as a plunger on the Turf, and who, I believe, died some little while back when out on a shooting expedition. Rum thing happened to me the night before last.' said he, as he stood in our shop. I was a bit worried over some heavy bets I'd laid, and dreamed at night that,standing in "the rine'," I felt something on my hand,and looking down,l saw 'I had a black bracelet on my wrist, on which, in white figures, were the num- bers, "3, 1, 5." Waking up in the morning, I thought no more of the matter till I arrived at Gatwick '—or Kempton Park or Goodwood, I really forget which he said—'and then as I was worrying to think what I should back, my dream of the night before came to me Instantly I made up my mind. I got a race card,backed No. 3 in the great race heavily to win, and put substan- tial sums on Nos. 1 and 5 for a place, and in each case. the thing came off. Had I left my bets as they were, I should have been thousands out.' And to commemorate the event, he ordered, and, I believe, wore ever after, a thin band of oxidised silver with the lucky numbers, 3, 1, 5,' in white enamel upon it. So you see, sir, -whenever a man wears a bracelet, if it isn't put on just for mere effeminate show, you may be sure the ornament has some sort of a history.—" Cassell's Saturday Journal."

div.head: MAKING MONEY.
div.p: MAKING MONEY.

Where are we to look for new outlets? Inventors and discoverers are, says " Cas:eTs Family:Magazine," th saviours of society. The photographic art is modern enough to be a useful case in point. Photographers in- creased 41 per cent. from 1871 to 1881, and 59 in the following decade. New industries give rise to new wastes ; and it was not long before it was discovered that the precious metal used in the developing solutions could be recovered, or that the yolk of eggs,whose white was employed in providing albuminised paper, need not be thrown away as valueless, but would realise hand- some prices from pastry cooks. The history of waste products, indeed, is extremely instructive, and very pertinent to this article. Lord Palmerston declared that, "dung was only gold in the wrong place." In some cases by-products have become the main products. Gas tar—truly an unpromising material—now yields numberless products, as any science primer shows. From even more unlikely sources scents are obtained. As Lord Playfair once said : "Many a fair forehead is damped with the huile de 271111 e-ileum without knowing that Its essential ingredient is derived from the drainage of a cowhowe." To the French belongs the greatest credit in discovering, new means of making money. The Parisian chiffonnier is much sharper than his London brother, who does a queer trade in cigar ends and old hats, boots, etc., which are" faked "to look as good as new. It was a Parisiao who first utilised old sardine tins, long regarded as worthless. He extracted the solder, and utilised the tin in the manufacture of toys and for beating into furni- ture. Another Parisian, an old soldier, collected old crusts and made them into bread crumbs for cooks, and in time started a place of business, whence were sup- plied c-routes an pot, so dear to connoisseurs in soups. One of the latest novelties reported from across the Channel is a process for washing packs of playing cards and renewing the edges. Unless the Government inter- fere, this industry is likely to bone me a large one,for duty on cards makes the constant purchase of new pack a considerable item in th‘g accounts of restaurants and other places of public resort.
THE CZAR AS A STAMP COLLECTOR.

Some grieve for the Czar because they loved him, some because he was their King, some in that a Prince of Peace has passed away. To the "Stamp Collectors' Fortnightly " the chief concern is as to the fate of the late Czar's magnificent collection of stamps. The Czar, we are told, was never able, personally, to take a very active interest in stamps. He was a stamp collector only by proxy. His secretaries acted as his agents in this matter. A Hamburg dealer has for years acted as the Czar's collecting agent in Germany. There is a story told of a Wisconsin boy who, when the U.S. Columbian stamps appeared, saved up his pocket money to Ret an unused set to send to the Czar. His Majesty, delighted with the ingenuous letter that accompanied the gift, returned the compliment by sending his little American correspondent s complete set of untved Russian stamps, from the earliest issues to the present time.

A CERTAIN MINISTER, who knew he was not very popular, was one day accosted by one of his old parishioners who said: "Oh, sir, I do like the day when you preach." The minister, some- what surprised, said: "My good woman, I am glad to hear it; there are too few like you. But, why do you like it when I preach l" "Oh, sir," she replied, "when you preach there is always plenty of room, and I get a good seat." -

div.head: ARE HORSES ARTFUL?
div.p: ARE HORSES ARTFUL?

"Both horses pulling the same ?" said the omnibus- driv,r to a writer in " Cassell's Saturday Journals." "No, sir, not by a long way. Horses is like men : some of 'em is artful, and others ain't. Them as is artful, don't do much work, but gets credit for doing a good deal ; them as ain't do more than their share, and don't get no extra credit for it. Now look at these two of mine. I've driven 'ern for twelve months now, and I know 'em. Which do you think is doing the most work, the white one ? I know'd you'd say that ; anybody would to lok at 'ern. Be seems to he doing it all, but th it's his artfulness. Be gets furthest into. the collar, but if you put your finger under it, you would find it quite loose. He only just hangs on it, enough to keep the traces tight. The brown horse ain't as far into his collar, but I reckon if you put your finger there, you'd get a had pinch. He's moving the 'bus, and that's why I always Lit the white when I whip up. You notice when we've pulled up, and are starting again, 'he white horse is the first to get forward, but he only goes just far enough to tighten the traces, and then waits for the : brown to start the 'bus. It's just the same with nearly all 'bus hor,;(,—you never find a fair division of labour between a 'pair. They know at a yard which are the gootl ones, and so they put good and bad together."

_ALLEGED OUTRAGEOUS ASSAULT ON A GIRL AT RUNCORN.

At the Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. F. J. Norman, on Friday morning, a boy named John Harold Curzon, 13 years of age, residing with his parents in Vine-st., Runcorn, was charged on a warrant with inflicting grievous bodily harm upon Elizabeth Lyon, five years of age, daughter of Eliztbeth and John Lyon, 67, Shaw-st., Runcorn.—Mr. A. Linaker, solicitor, defended the prisoner, who pleaded not guilty.—Evidence in support of the charge was given by the mother of the child, Dr. McKenzie, P.C. Gregory, Herlsert Pritchard, Vine-st., Edward Hayes, Shaw-st., and Thomas Davies, Handley-st. the last three of whom are playfellows of the prisoner.—,lt was stated that on the afternoon of the 20th inst. the prisoner, with the playfellows named, were sitting round a small fire which they had kindled on some waste ground at the back of Shaw-street. Curzon called the little girl, an 0. she sat by his side. Afterwards, the prisoner is alleged to have put some red-hot cinders on to a/ small piece of slate and to have then thrown them at the child, burning her severely about the lower part a the body. He then ran away asking Pritchard to go with hhn and not to say anything about the matter. The child ran home screaming to her mother, who subsequently called in Drs. Robinson and McKenzie. The latter gentleman, in his testimony, asserted that when he first saw the child on the 26th of October the burn appeared to be a very severe one, and added that the injary, if it had been allowed to develops' would have maimed the girl for life. The child was then doing well and would probably completely recover in a week or more.—Mr. Linaker very briefly addressed the bench, alluding to certain apparent discrepances in the various statements of the younger witnesses. He did not consider the evidence strong enough to commit the lad to the Sessions.—Mr. Norman on the other hand thought the testimony was quits strong enough and committed the prisoner to the next adjourned Quarter Sessions of Chester which will be held at Knutsford some time in January.—Bail was granted in two sureties of £25 each, the father of the prisoner being accepted for both.
EARLESTOWN BAPTIST CHURCH
ANNIVERSARY.

MR. SAM WOODS, M.P. ON SELF GOVERNMENT'. . Special services in connection with the anniver- sary of the Earlestown Baptist Church were held on Sunday, morning and evening. At both services practical discourses were given by the Rev. C. F. Aired, of Pembroke Chapel, Liverpool to crowded congregations. In the afternoon an address was delivered to a packed audience by Mr. Sam Woods, MX., on "Knowledge is power.' The Rev. C. F. Aked presided. Mr. Woods said if they only knew the meaning of the word knowledge, what a depth of meaning there was in that word. Having recounted in detail what benefits would accrue to mankind,from a knowledge of numerous sciences and laws of nature, he alluded to the virtue of temperance. The knowledge of temperance and a practice of temperance became first of all a power against disease, an influence and a power against poverty, and he believed that the lack of temperance was a great barrier to the human progress in the world. He knew of nothing in his experience that so hampered the progress and pros- perity of the human family, as the intemperance of the working families of this country. He was pleased how- ever to see rays of hope. Every day they lived they saw many going from the ranks of the intemperate, and be- coming temperate men. What kind of knowledge was most essential? There were many kinds of knowledge. There was a knowledge, which it was not beneficial for them t acquire. Same people would say, "you ought to go to college you ought to get well versed in the various language of the world." Though that was of great advantage to the possessor, yet it was not the kind of knowledge it was most essential man should know. He believed that what a man entering into life ought to know, and know accurately was three things—he ought to know whore he was, what kind of world he was in, what were the laws which governed that world. There was sufficient in this for a lifetime of thought. There were in this country a million of workingmen who could not get a day's employment. There were another million of men in this country who were living on the verge of starvation, who were not getting sufficient to maintain their families as they ought to be maintained. When they went to London, Liverpool, Manchester and any of the great cities and towns of this country, and when they saw the depths of poverty that met them at every stride they took, they began to think that it was a prob- lem which would have to be solved in the near future. These were facts which could not be denied. He was quite aware that intemperance had a lot to do with the poverty they saw on every hand. There was work for all of them to do, and there was no time for trifling, and it behoved each one of them to use those talents which God had given them for the good of their fellow men. First of all they ought to possess the knowledge and then apply it for the good of mankind. What had they given them in the last session of Parliament? They had a weapon put in their hands which they could not only use for their own influence, but for the furtherance of Christianity. They had a lever put in their hands to be used for the general good of mankind, and that was by taking an active part in the local administration of their town. What was being done in all parts of the country ? Rates were raised to the very highest pitch, and local affairs of the township were being grossly mismanaged because the people had had no right to share in those affairs. For the next election in connection with the district councils they were running at least 60 or 70 men from the ranks of labour round Wigan and the out townships. But that was only the beginning—it was only the thin end of the wedge. (Hear, bear, and applause.) He concluded by again urging all of them to take an interest in the local government of their districts. The collections during the day amounted to £ll 17s. 61
A. RUNCORN TAILOR'S CRUELTY TO

div.head: HIS WIFE.
div.p: HIS WIFE.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions before Messrs. Henry Reynolds and T. Rigby on Monday morning Joseph Littlemore, tailor, Greenway-road, Runcorn, was summoned by his wile, Hannah, for assault- ing her on the 29th Uctober.—Mr. ;Joseph Burton, solicitor, appeared for the complainant, and the defendant, who denied and then admitted the charge " in one sense," conducted his own case. Mr. Burton stated that on the night of the date named the defendant retired to bed a few minutes before his wife. When she went to the room, with the intention also of going to bed, the defendant at once began to abuse her. He struck her, without provocation, with considerable force on the left shoulder, and tried to put her out of the room. She held on to the bed rail. as he had threatened to throw her downstairs. At length she went downstairs and, taking her baby with her, went out of the house. This was at twelve o'clnck at night, and she remained out for some time until her mother lot her in again through the back door. On the previous day (Sunday) at noon, he again assaulted her.—Mr. Burton asked their worships to grant the wile a separation order as her husband had, without doubt, been guilty of an aggravated assault upon her. He would also venture to ask f,r a substan- tial amount to be paid to her weekly for the mainten- ance of her seven children and herself. Hannah Littlemore, wife Of the aefendant, supported her solicitor's statement, and added that she had been married nineteen years. At noon on Sunday her hus- band took a knife from the table and attempted to cut her throat. So far as she could judge her husband earned °utile average £2 per week at his business. Almost daily she was abused by her husband. (Defendant in- terrupting : Yes ; through your mother). In answer to questions by her husband, complainant denied having attempted to cut his throat with a knife. Neither had she picked up a poker with the intention of " knocking his brains out." Her mother had been very good and kind to her, and was not the cause of all the trouble between herself and her husband.—ln reply to Mr. Burton she said that in August last her husband had kicked her in the lower part of the both', and Dr. McDougall, who attended her, had remarked -that if the kick had been delivered lower down it would have Caused her instant death. Hannah rover, mother of the last witness, supported her daughter's statement. She did not see her daughter pick up a knife on the night of the 29th October, and threaten to cut her husband's throat. Neither did she hear her threaten him in any other way on a subsequent occasion. Isaac Littlemore, son of the defendant, also spoke to the assault upon his mother by his father, and to the latter attempting to cut his mother's throat with a knife On the previous Sunday. Defendant denied that he had ever lifted his hand against his wife, and insisted that the witnesses had swore falsely against him. Flis wife had picked up a Poker on the 29th October and had threatened to knock his brains out. This was why he would not have herin the bedroom on the night of the 29th October. She had also said she would poison him. He only earned £1 per week on the average. The trouble -throughout his whole married life had been caused by his mother-in- law. The magistrates imposed a fine of 10s. and 15s. 61. costs, or fourteen days hard labour. They also granted a separation order, the defendant to pay his wife 18s. Per week for her own and her children's maintenance.

He saw in one of the daily papers that meat which could not be disposed of in Warrington, St. Helens, or Liverpool was always taken to Earlestown, where it could always ho disposed of, and he said the' Sinitary Authorities should insist imon a persistent inspection of all food. sold on the market, and commit any person found selling diseased meat. (Hear, hear.) For dealing with infectious diseases he said, they wanted a disinfeeeing apparatus, and if they had this, it would do without the necessity of an infectious hospital. Why could they not have a cottage hospital? Jr would be of infinitely more service than an infectious .diseases hospital for a district like that Alluding to the water supply, he said they had a fair water, but it was not perfect, and the pressure was not geod. One of the first duties of the District Council ought to be the obtaining of a fire engineond the forma- tion of a volunteer fire brigade. Referring to sewage matters, he said they weuld have to erect a sewao deetructor somewhere, and if they returned him, as representative for ‘Varerave, he would use his his best endeavours to prevent that destructor being put any- where near Wargrave. Flo consiJored the baths and washhouses act should he adopted. If the district went on increasing, and if they could get a bath in this dis- trict, it would he a great boon to the neighbourhood. He alluded to the Burials Acts, and said there were in- justices in connection vith the Cemetery which required remedying. ( opla Mr. E. Marcie in proposing that Dr. Mouncey was a fit and proper person to repreeent the Wargrave ward on the Newton District Council, and that they use every means to secure his electien,said he thought Dr.Mouncev would he the right man in the right place.—Mr. R. Ambrose seconded, and Mr. Gosling supported.—The resolutien was put and unanimously carred.—A vote of thanks to the chairman terminated the meeting.

La Sposina, and Mr. Wareham II Marinajo. The concert opened with the orchestra playing Pront's " Triumphal March." Then followed two selections by Mr. Carl Fuchs, solo vi.doncello, one being an aria from J.S. Bach, and the other an intermezzo from Lab. These he ex- ecuted with masterly skil!, and was loudly applauded. The recitatives entrusted to the two personators were rendered with the required taste and feeling, Miss A';water's expression being especially distinct. The choruses were capitally sustained, and Mr. F.H. Crossley is to b- complimented upon the good fruits of his teach- ing. 'The orchestral accompaniments were also very fine. An interval of ten minutes succeeded the close of the first part, and the second stage was opened with an overture from Mendelssohn entitled "Son and Stranger.' This was skilfully given, after which Mr. Edwin' I Wareham contributed the air " Salve ! Dimora—Oh I Hail ! Thou Pure," Gounod. Miss Atwater afterwards scored a big success by her vivacious rendering of the valse chantee " Nymphes at Sylvaius," H. Bembey, and responded to an enthusiastic encore by singing "I wouldn't, would you." The chorus then delivered a part song entitied " The River Floweth," Dr. Rogers. 'The next to engage the attention of the audience was Mr. Carl Fuchs, who deli,ghteci his audience by his in- terpretation of three items, namely, " Melody," (F. H. Crossley), ",Cradle Song," and " Village Song" (Popper). The 'cellist was rewarded by an extraordinary outburst of applause and was compelled to respond. Mr. Ware- ham sang "A May Morning" with praiseworthy expression, and after the orchestra had executed an intermezzo from Mascagni's " Cavalleria, Rusticana " in good style, Miss Atwater gave Millard's love song entitled "Waiting." For this she was loudly applauded. The orchestra and chorus then brought the programme to a conclusion by a joint rendition of "The Gallant Troubadour." The singing of the National Anthem terminated the proceedings. Much praise is due to Mrs. Kay, who accompanied on the pianoforte in her usual accomplished manner, to Mr. F. H. Crossley, the Society's efficient conductor, and to the remaining officers,all of whom have helped in some degree to bring about such a satisfactory beginning to the Society's season.
WM:GRAVE WARD,

In connection with the candidature of Mesrs. W. Davies and E. C. Pryor for Wargiav Ward, a tiliet- ing was held in the Wargrave scnools on Monday evening. Mr. J. Rodgers presided and thore were present on the platform, Nlessrs. D.l vi Pryor, _Ralson, Owen and Jones. There was a fair at•tend- ance of electors. . .

_ The Chairman said it gave him great pleasure to pre- side over that meeting, more especially seeing that the meeting was called under the auspices of the Ward (), in- mittee, and to support two eentlemen who had been brought out in the interests of labour. He then detailed the bringing together of the committee and said that a portion of the committee broke faith with the others,ev reason of their determination to supeert no other (len- didates than those selected by the Censervative Glob. He did not, however, object to their breakine faith with the committee, as it gave them an opportunity of assert- ing their manhod. ! Mr. W. Davies said the point with him and the committee in asking him to etetei was that the three gentlemen proposed last week, we, e employers of labour. The act was not framed that one p iiticul Ir vl.Bl should be represented, but every class. Provisien was made iii the act for Government by the peeple and for the people. In the rural parishes the ae.riculteeal latiourer stood on a level with the parson and the squire, as they had an equal interest in the affairs of the parish, and OTI the same grounds why should not workingmen have a voice in the matter. Had they no interest, at stake? DII tlapy not live in the district? He had no objection to employers but, he said, all classes should be represented on the Board, and workingmen should have a share in the government of their parish. (Hear, hear.) Ever since he could remember he had taken an active pert in all social movements for the benefit of his on elms, and so long as he could see anything for the social imer aeons-et and advancement of the workingealasses that was the object he should have in view. (Hear, hear.) A good ! deal was said last week about a petition, aid it was intimated that it was that petition which ! had brought them together, and not the Dis- trict Councils Act. (Laughter.) He thought the employers of labour, arid the large re tepa.yers of all Sections if they were honest, would -day *that a vv,,rking. man should be sent in for every ward. (Bear, hear.)_ Referring to the conditions of, labour, lie said that at. meeting of the Lancashire Counts. Council, the other week, a contract for some work had to be given outeand a Mr. Postlethwaite moved a resolution that a 1 men employed on the job should have fair conditions Of lab our. Mr. Snape seconded, and 36 voted for it, bet it was lost by a large majority. He would like Mr. • Berren the Councillor for Newton to say on which side he vo-0. (Hear, hear.) He referred to the sewage and water question, and said if they approved of his candidature, and by their votes elected him to the Council he should do what he could to the best of his ability on the lines laid down. (Applause.) Mr. E. C. Pryor, in addressing the meeting, referred to the new Act, and said they would notice that the in- tention of the:framers of the Abt:was to make the repre- sentation as wide and diversified as possible, every householder being eligible for a seat on the Board, and electors being able to vote without fear or -favour, by ballot. The cottager and workman and general house- holder residing in the ward had an equal right to repre- sentation, and he protested most strongly against any class or party trying to monopolise that or anv other ward. (Hear, hear.) He referred to several vestions in what is known as the candidates catechism, such as "Common rights," 'I Post Office," " Reading rooms," " Technical Education" and explained his views upon them. Mr. J. Cerdingley moved that Messrs. Davies and Pryor be accepted as candidates to represent Wargrave Ward on the District Council—Mr. W. Haleon seconded.—The resolution was put and carried with two dissentients. In answer to a question by Mr. S. Barrett, with regard to finding free places in schools, Mr. Davies said that personally he was in favour of School Boards, because it gave the management of the schools into the hands of the people. He said anyone could have free education, who applied for it.—Mr. Pryor said as long as the volun- tary sehools ware giving satisfaction, and there were sufficient free places, he did not see the necessity for needless expense in forming a School Board. A vote of thanks to the Chairman, moved by Mr. Davies,and seconded y Mr. Pryor having been accorded the meeting dispersed. WAR G R AVE WARD.
DEATH OF MR,. CHA RLES LISTER, OF
LYMM.

The death of Mr. Charles Lister, Registrar of the Manchester County Court, took plate on Monday morning at his residence, Agden, .Ball, Lymm, from inflammation of the lungs. Mr. Lister was admitted a solicitor in 1864. In 1876 he was appointed to ect in conjunction with the late Mr. Kay as registrar of the Manchester County Court, and a few weeky ago, consoqu,,Tt on the demise of Mr. Kay.tie was appointed Foie registr r. fie was hardly less distinguishod in his office of Registrar of an important court than as a prison refcrtner and philanthropist. He effectively directed public attention to the question of " first offonders." He wati strongly convinced that greater clemency should be shown to those who for the first time were placed on their trial, Mr. Lister was a Conservative and a churchman. In Lymin and the district he was actively associated with the Conservative parts ,and in 1889 was selected as their candidate for the seat on the Cheshire County Council for the Lvmm Division. He defeatel his opponent, Mr. J. L. Stelfox,by a large majority and at the next election in 1892 he was returned unopposed. As a churchman he was warmly attached to the venerable parish church of Rostherne, and at the restoration of the fabric some years ago he placed a hands,sme stained glass window in the Ag.den Chapel. He was an active justice of the peace for the city of Manchester, and was on the Commission for Cheshire. Derbyshire. and Lancashire. It is probable that he -you'd before long have held the highest position in Cheshire—that of High Sheriff. A few years age he did good service to the Corporation of Manchester by presiding over a tribunal which was formed to consider certain charges against the administration of the affairs of the Health Department. He leaves a widow and three children. References to the worth of the deceased were made at various courts with which he was connected.
RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY.
OPENING OF TITE SEASON.

The Runcorn Musical Society opened their (seventh) 1894-5 season in the Public Hall, Run- corn, on Tuesday evening with a grand concert. There was a very large audience present, the seat- ing accommodation on the floor of the hell being entirely utilised, whilst the galleries were likewise well patronised. The concert was also a success from a musical standpoint. The committee very fortunately fixed upon a trio of talented artistes, and were success- ful in securing their services for this occasion. These were Miss Regina Atwater, a prima donna of Amp/ nationality, who is fast reaming fame as a soprano singer of the American school ; Mr. Edwin Wareham, a prominent tenar ; and Mr. Carl Fuchs, a 'cellist of coaspicalous ability. It might he interesting to some of our readers to kno-v that " This talented 'cellist was born in 1365, at Offen- bach-en-Main, Germany. When eight years old he re- ceived his first instructions on the 'cello from Riedel. later he entered the Frankfort 'Conservatoire and hp.. came a pupil of Crossman. Soon afterwards Davidoff, the great 'cello player, heard him play, and invited him to go to St. Petersburg. Since then Fuchs has beers heard at Halle's Liverpool Philharmonic Gentlemen's Concerts, Glasgow Chorkl Union, &e,., creating everv- where the greatest, furore ." This trio fully met the ex- pectations of the Society, Miss Atwater and Carl Fuchs being, perhaps, the two prime favourites, if distinction is to be at all permitted. The chorus singers, who num- bered about one hundred, are deserving of the highest praise for the efficient rendering of their various parts, but it is to be somewhat regretted that the orchestra, which was made up of a number of skilful instrumenta- lists, was, to a certain extent, too strong for them. Had the orchestra been a little lighter, the voices of the choristers might have been heard perhaps to greater advantage. However, be that as it may, the concert proved a decided musical success. The first portion of the proceedings was devoted to the interpretation of Sir A. Sullivan's dramatic cantata "On shore, on sea," which was composed expressly for,and Torformed at the opening of, the London International Exhibition. The persons renresented in the cantata were :—La Sposina, a Riviera Woman ;II Marinajo.a Genoese ; chorus of Riviera Women, Genosese Sailors, and Moorish Sea Rovers. The action passes in the 16th century at a port of the Riviera, near Genoa. and on hoard of a Genoese and Moorish galley at sea The second portion of the concert was of a miscellane ous description. In the cantata,Miss Atwater pensonated

A meeting in connection with the candidature of Dr. Mouncey for the Wargrave ward, was held in the War- grave school on Tuesday evening. Mr. flalson presided and there were present on the platform Messrs. Gosling Martin, Ambrose, and Williams. Dr. Mouncey after explaining shortly the aims of the District Councils Act said each district councillor would be the representative of every ratepayer directly or in- directly. Speaking on the question of common rights he said the new act said not only had the new District Council the power of seeing after those matters, but that it should be their duty to see after the protection of all roadside wastes and open footpaths for the use of the people. With regard to road making,in that di3trict, he said there were several places where houses had been built for several years, and in spite of them being so long, there were no proper roadways,which was a shame to any community. What the District Council ought to see to, was that those roads, where dwellings were numerous, and had been built along time, ought to be properly laid. If he was elected to the District Council he would do all he could to help forward the paving of roads, the taking over all roads which were partly private and putting roads generally in proper order. The District Council would have u-,nsiderable power over education. In that district they had got three very good schools which were in a good condition, well managed, and the children were well educated, and he did not se why they wanted a School Board, but if the schools went down, and there was not sufficient accommodation, then it would be the duty of the District Council to provide school accommodation, and to see that every working man had a thorough education for his children. Per- sonally he thought the voluntary schools did as well for the children as any Board school, and he would say they should do without a School Board as long, as possible. (Hear, hear.) With regard to the Sanitary matters,there was one thing, which-had come practically to his know- lecige,and which had stru-k him,and that was the great prevalence to disFase due to eating bad meat, which every now and then broke out, and due to th- insuffi- cient inspection of the market. During the time he had
NEW BOOKS, MAGAZINES, ETC.
Isecol

CASSELL AND CO.—Of all the cheap magazines suitable for every day reading (Sundays included) "The Quiver" is as good as the rest, and better than some. The November number forms the first part of a new volume, and provides us with light reading in the form of complete and serial stories, and for the more seriously-minded there are devo- tional and instructive papers by eminent clerical and other writers. The illustrations are excep- tionally fine, and the figure-drawing graceful ; the frontispiece being a pretty coloured picture of "A Daughter of the King." " Cassell's Universal Portrait Gallery "is the name of an important new work, of which the first part is published, this month. Twenty-four excellent cabinet-size portraits of celebrities of all sorts, printed from photographs, and each one accom- panied by a brief biographical sketch, are included for the moderate sum of sixpence. F'. WARNE AND Co.—From the prolific pen of the Rev. Silas K. Hocking we have "A Son of Reuben," with illustrations by H. R. Steer. " The " son" is George Lister, the second of a practical-minded manue.acturer, not a bit like his father, but a lazy " ne'er do weel," who had a soul above cotton and yarns, and hated the sight of looms. His own idea of himself was that he was a genius, destined some day to make his fortune in five minutes, and to startle the world of Art by conceiving and painting a picture—someday. To some extent he succeeds, but in the end gets his deserts, and after sinking to the lowest depths dies from the effects of an accident. The heroine is " a brown hedge-sparrow among the birds," a sweet, loving, cheerful girl, atoning for any lack of artistic charm by the naturalness and simplicity of her manner. After going through a world of trial and disappointment, she too gets her deserts, and marries the noblest character in the book with whom we suppose she "lived happy ever after- wards." There is an abundance of commonsense, pathos, sentiment, and humour, the interest i 3 well sustained, and the life-like characters are such as one may meet with any day, in this varied Lan- cashire of ours. The tone of the book is excellent, and like the rest of Mr. Hocking's stories, is emi- nently suitable for family reading. It appeals to what is best in our nature, and the influence of it can only be for good.

div.head: B E EKA MINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 10 1894.
div.p: B E EKA MINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 10 1894.
RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

Mr. James Pritchard presided over the monthly meeting of the above Board which was held on Tuesday evening in the Town Hall, Runcorn. There were also present the Rev. Canon M. Wood, Dr. McDougall, and Mr. George Moss, clerk. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE. The Clerk read the minutes of two prPvi ous meetings of the School Attendance Committee which showed that 66 parents had been summoned before the committee, 58 of whom had appeared. It was recommended that proceedings be taken against 13.—The minutes were adopted.

div.head: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT.
div.p: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT.

The minutes of the School Management Committee's last meeting showed that the Clerk had submitted a return, which was to tin sent to the House of Lords, having reference to the religious instruction imprtrted .to the scholars at the Board schools. The committee had approved of the return and had ordered it to be forwarded. They also recommended that 160 bibles be purchased for the Greenwav-road Schools, 100 for boys Xnd 60 for girls. That a kindergarten table be obtained from the Mill Brow Infants' School, at a cost of £1 ; and that other purchases of minor importance be made on behalf of the evening school.—On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Dr. McDougall, the minutes were confirmed.
NEWTON BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

At the monthly meeting of the above Board which was held at the Earlestown Town Hall on Monday, there were present Mr. J. W. Emmett (chairman), Col. McCorquodale, Messrs. G. Ratcliffe, T. Ormand, P. McMahon, P. Thompson, T. Foster, W. Coßingwood, E. T. Evans, R. Brierley,and (clerk and surveyor).

div.head: ABSENCE OF THE LAW CLERK.
div.p: ABSENCE OF THE LAW CLERK.
Mr. Emmett announced that Mr. ViTorsley, the law clerk, was unable to be present owing to his being hurriedly called to London.
THE "COMMON."

The Chairman announced that the law clerk had ob- tained legal opinion respecting that question of building on Newton Common. He mayed that the counsel's opinion be referred to the Highways Committee for con- sideration.—Mr. Ratcliffe seconded, and the motion was carried.

div.head: HIGHWAYS COMMITTEE.
div.p: HIGHWAYS COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of this C)mmittee, a letter was read from Mr. Thos. Peatts asking permission to build on the land opposite his shops in Market-st. It was resolved that the same be deferred for the opinion of the law clerk and that such applications be accompanied with a plan of the same, and of the premises adjoining. The following report was ordered to be entered on the minutes :—" October, 1894. To the Highways and Sanitary Committee. Gentlemen.—Your Committee appointed to attend the Sanitary Congress at Liverpool held September 26, were represented by myself,and Mr. Brierley. At the discussion on the use of destructors for disposal of town's refuse from which much information was obtained and an inspection was made of destructors at work in a densley populated locality near Vauxhall-road Liverpool from the burning of the refuse at a high tem- perature. Steam and electric light were also produced without causing any nuisance to the neighbourhood either from the destructors or the chimney. We also visited a destructor plant in progress of erection, in the highly suburban district of Toxteth Park. (Signed) Geo. Ratcliffe." The following plans were submitted and approved : R.B. Toft, additions to house, 66, Cross- lane ; Mrs. J. Starkie, 8 cottages. off Market-street (con- ditionally) ; Mr. J. G. Walton, 6 cottages, Athol-street. Mr. Gregory's report was read and appro. _!d. The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. G Ratciiffe, ,nded by Mr. McMahon.

At the meeting mf this committee, the present cost of gas and charges of meter hire were considered, and it was recommended that the price of gas to all but auto- matic consumers be reduced one penny per 1,000 feet ; that the meter hire for two light meters be reduced to 4d. per quarter, and that the hire of all other meters be re- duced 50 per cent, and that such reductions be allowed to the consumers for the current quarter ending Decem- ber next, The committee also recommended that a loan of £2,000 be borrowed on security of the Gas Works and rents to meet the overdraft on permanent works for new mains, meters, etc. An application was read from Mr. Astley King to be authorised as a gas and water fitter for the district. It was resolved that the applica- tion be acceded to so long as he complied with present and future regulations or the Board.—Mr. Emmett moved, and Mr. Ratcliffe seconded the passing of the minutes.—Mr. Forster regretted that the 2d. which was raised upon the gas last year was not although taken off. Mr. Emmett said that the committee would be very glad to do so if they could, but unfortunately, they could not afford. The price for coal was higher than it was before the strike.—The minutes were passed unanimously.

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of this committee held on October 15th, Mr. Ball, the school attendance officer, read the quar- terly statement, of attendances ending September. From it, it appeared that the number on the books was 2.556, average attendance, 2,157, percentage. 84i-. The cor- responding numbers last year were 2.580, 1,945, and_ 75 2-s—Mr. Ratcliffe moved, and Mr. Ormand seconded the adoption of the minutes, which were passed unani mously.

div.head: LETTING OF THE TOWN HALL.
div.p: LETTING OF THE TOWN HALL.

In pursuance of notice given at the previous meet- ing, Mr. Ormand moved the following resolution "Notwithstanding the foregoing rates of payment (for the letting of the Town Hall), it shall be lawful for the chairman for the time being of the Board or District Council, upon the written application which shall be signed by not less than ten ratepayers, and which ap- plication shall state the time and object of the proposed meeting, to allow the use ef the assembly room or any committee room except the Board room, to bona•fide ratepayers, for the purpose of holding meetings for con- sidering the candidature or promoting the election of members to the District Council or District Poor Law Guardians, or any matter of vital interest to the ratepayers, free from any charge or payment, except meetings having reference to Parliamentary elections or for use of members of Parliament or of candidates thereto.—Mr. Ratcliffe se- conded the motion, which was carried unanimously.— Mr. Emmett moved that the charge which was made for the meetings held prev!nusly,be refunded.—Mr.Ormand seconded, and Colonel McCorquodale supported the re- sQlution, which was passed unanimously.
THE DISTRICT COUNCILS ELECTIONS.

Mr. Ratcliffe moved, and Mr. McMahon seconded a resolution that the County Council be requested to fix the time for polling for the District Council from ten o'clock to eight, instead of from twelve to eight.—The resolution was Dassecl.—lt was also resolved on the motion of Mr. Emmett, seconded by Mr. Ormand, to appoint two polling stations for the Viaduct ward.

There are now three lady churchwardens actually holding office. All are dowagers—Lady Hindlip for a church in Worcestershire, near her residence ; Lady Fleathcote for North Ealing Church, in Hants ; and the Dowager Lady Londonderry for Machynlleth, in North Wales.

At Highgate Police Court, on Monday, the Rev. W. J. Jenkins, rector of Tillingham, and Senior Fellow of Minot College, was fined 403. and costs for assaulting a coal porter, and 60s. and costs for assaulting a con- stable.

At Burnley, on Monday, Annie Smith, a gipsy, was fined £5. and costs, with the alternative of a month's imprisonment, for defrauding Mrs. Walmsley,a married woman, of half-a-crown, two gold rings, a watch and chain, and other articles, by pretending to read the planets for her and to foretell her future.
