div.head: TOWN COUNCIL NOTES.
div.p: TOWN COUNCIL NOTES.

Neither the Mayor nor the Deputy-Mayor were in attendance at the Town Council meeting on Tues- day, and the senior alderman, Mr. Harrison, was ! elected to preside. There was no Jelay in getting !to business. Councillor Shaw, who has demon- strated very clearly since he entered the Council that he is not afraid of his own voice, was soon in evidence. He wished the Chairman of the Watch ! Committee to tell him all about the recent prosecu- tion of barbers for Sunday shaving—what the pro- secutions had cost and whether it was intended to prosecute other classes of Sunday traders. He was anxious for the small shopkeepers of the town, of whom, he said, there were over 400, some of whom were not "blessed with having a husband." He also read a portion of the seventeenth century Act of Parliament under which the pro- secutions had been made and declared positvely that the Act never mentioned a barber. Some of the other councillors seemed to be at a loss to understand why they should be bombarded with the questioning, and legal learning of Councillor Shaw, as it was stated that the Watch Committee had not prosecuted any barbers, had no intention of prosecuting any barbers, and had not had any costs to pay. In the end,Councillar Shaw intimated that he would raise the subject at the next meeting.

The next incident, illustrated the wonderfully exact knowledge which members of committees have of the business of the cDmmittees to which they belong. The Finance and Estate Committee recommended the acceptance of a contralt for printing and stationery, and Councillor Longton, who is a member of the committee,wanted to knpsv if the contract had been advertised in the usual way. Councillor James Fairclough, another mem- ber of the committee, declared that the contract had been advertised, but Mr. Longton was still sceptical upon the point, and as no other member of the committee present could definitely settle the difference, the Council as a whole was left without any conclusive testimony on either side.

Upon what principle are streets laid out in War- rington? That is a question upon which Councillor Bennett was anxious to have information upon,with especial reference to the streets in the Padgate-lane direction. He insinuated that the new thorough- fares in that part of the town had been laid out on a plan "which aimed at nothing and succeeded be- yond all expectation." And he and Councillor Woods complained that in Gorsey-lane the regula- tion forty feet width of street was not being al- alowed, but Councillor Shaw, who said he was building the two houses that, it was alleged, were not set far enough back, declared that a width of over !forty feet was being allowed. Councillor Hill next protested against the proposal of the Health Committee to take preliminary steps towards clos- ing some insanitary houses, but he was interrupted in the midst of a rather warm expostulation by Alderman Sutton asking if any of the houses be- longed to him. Mr. Hill retorted that that was " his business,' but Councillor Roberts followed the point up and obtained a ruling from the Town Clerk that persons pecuniarily interested in a ques- tion betore the Council could not take part in decid- ing it. Councillor Hill thereupon retired info obscurity, and left Councillor Smethurst in charge of the insanitary houses. This latter gentleman was assured that the Health Conimittee were bound to act upon the report of the Medical Officer in dealing with these defective dwellings. They had, however, no desire to harass property owners who still had the option of putting the houses into habit- able condition.

On the minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Com- mittee the most notable point was a startling mis- take in arithmetic made by Councillor Longton. The Committee proposed to buy two lots of fifty ventilator covers at £34 each lot, and Mr. Longton had apparently come to the conclusion that the price was to be £34 for each cover. When he be- gan to talk about a contemplated expenditure of £3,400 a sudden silence fell upon the Council, and the chairman of the Com mittve (Alderman Wright) asked for an explanation. It was then, of course, quickly seen where Councillor Longton had gone astray, and he was the subject of some banter in consequence. The system oi ventilating the sewers in Warrington was touched upon by Councillor Bennett and Councillor Beaman and the lattar made a vigorous weighty protest against it, refer- ring to the constant presence'of disease in the town.

In moving the Museum Committee's minutes, Councillor Roberts referred with satisfaction to the excellent start that had been made this season with the classes at the Technical Institute. Some dis- cussion also took place with regard to the altera- tions at the Cemetery hinted at in the report which was published last week, and on the minutes of the Town Hall, Park and Bath Committee, Councillor Roberts intimated that he should ,at a subsequent meting, ask for the total cost incurred in connec- tion with the removal of the wall and the erection of the gates in front of the Town Hall. The remain- ing business of the Council included some discus- sion as to the wretched.quality of the gas supplied to the townspeople on the previous Saturday, as to which the Chairman of the Gas Committee had no explanation; and also some talk with reference to the removal of the shop of the late Mr. 31arsh at the foot of Bridge-st. This latter subject was re- ferred back to the Committee, and it seemed to be understood that the Committee would recommend the pulling down of the shop in order to complete the widening of the street at that point.
WARRINGTON RURAL SANITAR.X
AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority took place at the Board mom of the Workhouse,on Friday. The Rev. G. F. Roberts presided, and there were also present, Mes,rs. W. Houghton, R. Heaton, A. Jolley.J. Dignum, Mather, Swinton; S. Sutton (clerk), W. Owen (surveyor), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), and F. Kerfoot (nuis- ance inspector.)

div.head: PROPOSED JOINT HOSPITAL COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE PROPOSED JOINT HOSPITAL COMMITTEE.

The CLERK read a report of the recent comference held at Preston, on the subject of a proposed smallpox Joint Hospital Committee.—Dr. Sephton said that he had spoken to Mr. Williams, who was secretary for the Joint Committee, which embraced Atherton Local Board. This Board was very much opposed to the scheme, and would not pledge itself to anythinr. The adjourned meeting of the committee would probably not be held until some agreement had been made with the Board.— The CHAIRMAN said that there was a unanimous feeling at the meeting at Preston, that joint action should be taken by the Authorities, although there was some dis- cussion as to whether it would not be practicable for the smallpox hospital to be assoc;ated with an infectious diseases hospital of a general character. But it was known that the Local Governtrn.nt Board would not con- sent to that.—The discussion then dropped.

MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORTS—SHIP CANAL STENCHES. Dr. SEPHTON reported that during the month there had been 28 births, and 11 death. The death rate equalled 9.4 per thousand, against 11.4, the aver- age for the last three months, and 17 for the corresponding: month of last year. The death rate for the zymotic diseases was niltagainst 1.8, the averaga of the last three months, and 1-6 the corresponding month of last year. During the month the following cases of infectious disease had been raported : scarlatina, 3 ; membraneous croup, 1; and typhoid fever, 2 cases He had to raport during the month also in September, there had been an intolerable stench proceeding from the Ship Canal. He suggested that the Clerk write to the Mersey and Irwell Joint Committee complaining of the matter.—The CLERK said that he had written a few months ago in consequence of complaints received from Dr. Gornall, but the committee replied that they had no power in the matter.—Mr. HEATON suggested that it was because the complaints arose from the tidal portion of the canal. The report was then adopted on the motion of Mr. HOUGHTON seconded by Mr. HEATON.

div.head: SURVEYOR'S REPORT.
div.p: SURVEYOR'S REPORT.

Mr. OWEN reported that with reference to Burton wood drainage, he had accepted the estimate of Messrs Beckett and Ca., amounting to £1,184, but had ordered the work not to be proceeded with until the money was in hand for the payment, and until possession of the land was given by the owner and the conveyance granted. The work of paving in Sankey Bridges was being pro- ceeded with satisfactorily. In accordance with the in- structions he had issued a certificate for the building plans of Mr. Gough's houses in SAnkey. The plan submitted for five cottages at Sankey was a;:proved aa far as the plans themselves were conc(red. No authority was given by this certificate to pollute with sewage any stream, ditch, or watercourse, which might be used by cattle for drinking purposes. No certificate for habita- tion would be issued for those houses until the drainage for them and the water supply for drinking purposes were entirely satisfactory to the Authority. The follow- ing plans were submitted to be approved: Mr. Thomas Garnett, additions to houses, Penketh ; Mr. Thomas Glover, toolmaker's shop, Penketh ; Me,isrs. Greenall Whitley, and Co., stable at Black Horse Inn, Sankey: Bridges: Mr. R. Forshaw, closet at the Fiddle Inn, Eartonwood.—The report was adopted.

FINDING WATER WITH THE DIVINING ROD.

If any seeptism, says a correspondent, has existed as to the man with the divining rod, it certainly has ciased in the county of Northumberland. On the Mit- ford estate especially it might be said of him as of the Hebrew legislator "he brought water out of the stony rock, so that it gushed out like rivers." Remote hamlets on the hill sides, which have hitherto had no supply other than that out of the ditches, are now rejoicing in the possession of wells to which the diviner directed them. The way in which he discovered he had the power of finding water is curieus. He had been ill, and for some purpose his blood was analysed. The doctor said to him that his blood contained more iron than ten ordinary men, and that he ought to be able to find water. This set him thinking, and his power has been so skilfully exercised, that he now falls into a fit of trembling directly he st3nds above the water supply, though it be at a depth of sixty feet.

TIIE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 10, 1894.
ONE of the worst blots upon th o "Jew-Baiting." reign of the late CZAR is the per-

secution to .which he subjected the Russian Jews. This persecution is one of the most lamentable incidents in the history of man- kind. "Jew-baiting" has, it is true, been only too common at one time or other in all European countries, and even now there are occasional out- breaks of popular prejudice against the Hebrews in Germany and Austria. But in these two countries " Jew-baiting " is not countenanced by the Government; on the other hand,it is repressed with more or less severity. But in Russia how different it has been! Persecution has been car- ried on with all the rigour and persistency of an irressistible autocracy. The late CZAR certainly deserves the title of the champion "Jew-baiter," fully as much as that of the pre- server of the peace of .Europe.. As one writer forcibly declares, "the vilest pariahs in India may be almost said to live in a paradise of social and legal equality compared with the Hebrew subjects of the CZAR. Every Jewish alien has long ag,9 been expelled from Russia, while the Russian Semites subject to the CZAR have been hunted and lashed, like so many escaped cattle, back to their-pen or pale of settlement,their huge Ghetto, where, crowded to excess in the /ties and townlets, they have such a desperate struggle for existence, for dear life, as can only be , compared to the savage welter of the wild animals ' of Africa, that are driven by the natives into vast pits, where they can be speared and despatched at leisure." In one year alone, 1891, more than 60,000 Jews fled to the United States, and it is said that there are non, as many as 200,000 Jews in New York alone. Unless the present CZAR reverses or mitigates the policy of his predecessor, there appears to be before the unhappy Muscovite Jews only the dismal alternative of extermination or emigration. By embracing the orthodox religion of their oppressors the Jews might escape the pains and penalties that are now inflicted upon them, but it is said by those who speak on their behalf that-they will never submit to that.
THE temperance p.lrty of Wzia._ 'the Licensing ington are fairly entitled to Appeals. congratulate themselves the result of the licensing appeals. decision of the local magistrates been
virm The

ref using the licenses has _ up- held in one case though it has been reversed in the other. The " Pelican " will still continue to do business as one among the many public-houses around Market Gate, but the " Swan " will now, we presume, be finally closed. That is at least one step towards ridding Warrington of its super- abundance of licensed houses. In the opinion of most of the townspeople, as well as of the borou.;11 bench, the town could have got along very well without either of these puhlie-houses, but the county justices wil:ed otherwise. Ou the whole, the result is not unsatisfactory. It was, consider- ing the way in which Quarter Sessions generally deals with these cases, too much to expect that the refusal of the license would be confirmed in both cases. It would, On the other hand, have been no overwhelming surprise if both appeals had been allowed, however much the fact might have been deplored. The whole procedure in connection with these appeals affords a weighty argument in favour of licensing reform. At the present time a local bench is apparentiy at full liberty to flood a , district with licenses, to • place the temptations oi

In connection with these licenses it is much easier to give than to take away, even though tho giving may be a public evil while the taking away is a public advantage.

THR evidence given at the Local Arrangements Union . Government inquiry at Warring- ton on Saturday was all in favour of retaining the townships of Latchford (extra municipal), Grappenhall and Thelwall in the Warrington Union. The proposal is, of course, to sever the townships from Warrington and add theta to the Runcorn Union. There seems to be no reason for the adoption of such a course„ except that by lopping off these townships the Warrington Union would be entirely in Lan- cashire, and the ratepayers of Grappenhall and Thelwall would have to pay a somewhat reduced rate. All the "natural affinities,' if we may use the phrase in this connection, f the townships. are with Warrington. The distr tis essentially a suburban one and most of th residents have- business connections with the town. If any con- sideration is to be given to the poor—and that really ought to be a prime consideration in con.. nection with the arrangements of a union—there is absolutely nothing to be said for the severance of the townships. The poor will be practically cut off from all relief if relief is only to be ob- tained at Dutton Workhouse where the Runcorn Board of Guardians hold their fortnightly meet- ings. The decision of the Local Government. Board will, under the circumstances, be awaited with much interest.

Tun evidence which is being. given at the inquiry into the loss. of the New Zealand passenger steamer, Wairarapa, and over one hundred of its, passengers and crevr,is not pleasant reading. One. is accustomed to expect something better than is
A Shipwreck.
here disclosed from British seamen. In the first, place it is alleged that the vessel, though freighted
with so many lives, was driven at full speed through a dense fog and near a dangerous coast,
and that all the usual precautions under such cir- cumstances were neglected. And then when the

vessel had gone upon the rocks the crew displayed. a sad lack of discipline, to say nothing of chivalry. It seems to have been a rush for life in which the. weakest were the sufferers. The chief officer is, reported to have admitted that lie left a mother and child partly submerged in a corner while he

himself was pulled up into the rigging by the. steward. The unfortunate woman and child were then washed away. Another of the crew deposes. that no orders were given to place tIR, women and children in the boats first. It was a case of "everyone for himself." In one instance, a life-- raft was seen to float out to sea with twenty per- sons on board and no attempt at rescue was made.. Altogether, the wreck of this colonial steamer will be the theme of one of the most piteous and least, heroic tales of the sea.

ELECTIONS in the United States. The American Elections, seem to be influenced by a prin-. eiple of " see-saw " even more than: they are in England. At the last elections the, Republican party was more than decimated by a_ great reaction in favour of the Democrats. The. elections which have taken place this week show that the political pendulum has again swung in an, opposite direction, as the Democrats have been heavily beaten in all parts of the country. What does this Democratic reverse signify ? Does it *mean a return to the high Protectionism which was embodied in the McKinley tariff when the Republicans were last in power ? These are questions of some importance to this country, and in those interested in the export trades. Fortu- nately, there are several reasons for believing that the Republicans have not fought and won this question on promises of more stringent protection. Some of their leading man have emphatically declared in the course of the election campaign that they had ,no in4intion to return to McKinleyism, and it seems to be generally con- cluded, even by the Republicans themselves, that what the people of the United States now want is a cessation of the tinkering with the tariff which has been a disturbing element for som years now. ,i3.tit;:y,ikkam&.

She struck and kicked e Peter several times and as she would not desist when told he took her to the police station. Here she again e assaulted Peter, kicking him until he screamed, and using very had language throughout.—P.C.Barnett gave corroborative evidence and Inspector Spinke deposed to witnessing the scene at the police station, and said that he had had also tried to get her to a lodging-house becausee • , of the children, but in the end he had beGn compelled to , lock her up. On one occasion when the Inspector went for her a'. Ciolberne she was very drunk and smashed a chair betore their eyes. ILLNESS MR. S. B. CHADWICK, J.P., OF RUNCORN. The recovery ef Mr. S. B. Chadwick, J.F., who is at present suffering from a severe illness at his Kingsley residence, is becoming every day more improbable. His medical attendant, Dr. McDougall, is bestowing all his skill upon the suffering gentleman, and it is sincerely trusted that his endeavours will not be fruitless. LECTURE ON TENNYSON AT RUNCORN. At a weekly meeting of the members of the Bethesda Literary and Social Class, held on Tuesday evening, in the Lecture Hall of the Bethesda Church, the Rev. J. S. Simpson delivered a lecture on the poet Tennyson. There was not such a large attendance as usual, the counter-attraction at the Public Hall being perhaps the cause. div.head: RUNCORN FOOTBALLER INJURED.
div.p: A RUNCORN FOOTBALLER INJURED.

Albert West, a member of the second team of the Run- corn Rugby Football Club, met with a disagreeable accident whilst playing against the' Magazines" on Saturday afternoon last at Runcorn. He was one of the forwards, and during a bit of exciting play he was kicked on the head and sustained a serious scalp wound. Dr. McKenzie, who was psesent at the match, stitched up the wound, and has since then attended him again. West is now going on satisfactorily, and will soon *- able to fill his place again in the team. SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN UT- By. On Tuesday morning, between the hours of ten and eleven o'clock, an old man named Thomas Houghton, aged about 68 years, who resides in Lowlands-road, Runcorn, met with a very serious accident. Whilst new weighing machine was being fixed near the lay-by he was struck in the chest by a large stone which was suspended in the air at the end of a chain. His chest was crushed by the force of the blow, and he also sustained injury to his shoulder. He was rendered un- conscious and was taken home where he received prompt attention at the hands of Dr. Mangan, Runcorn. Late on Thursday he was found to be progressing as favour- ably as could be expected, though still suffering from severe shock and internal injuries. BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVRMENT CLASS, RUNCORN. On Wednesday evening the usual weekly meeting of the above class was held, the Chairman being Mr. T. Simister. There was a fairly large attendance. Mr. Fred. Hartland, of Widnes, read a paper entitled" Peace v. War "—a most striking array of facts and figures—in which the es,ayist denounced war of all kinds, and ad- vocated universal disarmament. A spirited discussion ensued in which Messrs. Peter Rigby, Ledstone, William Massey, and Pickthal traversed the writer's statements. His views, on the other hand, were upheld by Mr. J. D. Jones. The lecturer afterwards replied to his critics, and the meeting, which had proved of very great interest, then terminated. BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, RUNCORN. With the laudable object of augmenting the funds of the London Missionary Society,sermous will be preached in this church on Sunday morning and evening next, on the former occasion by the Rev. C. Clay, 8.A., of Lyrom and on the latter by the Rev. G. 11. Bondfield,trom Hong Kong. In the afternoon a service will be held for chil- dren, parents, and friends, when the last named gentle- man will deliver an address bn Monday evening a public meeting will be held with the same object. Mr. J. Prit- chard will occupy the chair, and addresses will be given by the Rev. G. H. Boudfield, and the Revs J. Richardson, from Madagascar. There will it is hoped, he a large congregation present at each event, and that liberal sub- scriptions will be given in order that the London Mis- sionary Society may receive that assistance of whic.:ll they are in sore need, and which will enable thdm to continue their good work. COLLIER'S is. BtrrrEs. is the gem in the market.—Advt. DEATH OF Mn. JOHN TEMPERLEY, RT,INCORN. It is with regret that we announce the death of Mr. John Temperley, late of 33, Lowlands-road, Runcorn, who died on Saturday evening in his sixty-first year. For several months he had been in failing health, but nevertheless, the news of his decease came as a shock to the various members of his family, as well as to a vstcle circle of friends and acquaintances. Mr. Temperley WF s a native of Runcorn, and for more than twenty years bad carried on business in Lowlands-road as a baker and confectioner. For nearly thirty years he had worked for the Wesleyan cause at the Cam- den Chapel having held the positions of class leader, chapel steward, and society steward. He had also been a local preaeher in the Wesleyan Circuit, and an advoc- ate of total abstinence. In politics he was a well-known Liberal, and took great interest in the transactions of the local Liberal party. The remains of the deceased gentleman were interred in the Runcorn Cemetery, Greenway-road, on Wednesday afternoon, a large num- ber of relatives and friends being present at the ceremony which was performed by the Rev. T. Brackenbury, superintendent Wesleyan minister. THE RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPERANCE AND THE GOTHENBURG SYSTEM.

A meeting of the members of the Runcorn Sons of Temperance took place on Saturday evening, Mr. George E. Sutton presiding. P; will be remembered that at the last meeting a discussion on the Gothenburg system was started and adjourned until this present meeting. Mr. Bisbrown resumed the discussion .saving that he was not

_ much in sympathy with the project, though he thought that the promoters, if they had faith in it, might try it on a small scale as a test. The adoption of such a plan ought not to interfere with any other remedial measures. Re approved of the Gothenburg scheme in one or two respects, AS there was total Sunday closing and shorter hours during the week, namely, from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m., but he contended that the apprehensions for drunkenne,S were more numerous in Gothenburg, in the ratio of the population .than in Liverpool and Cardiff. In conclusion Mr. Bisbrown said that Mr. Edward Goadby had gone to Gothenburg to make a special study of the licensing system, to which he had paid attention some years ago. This rreutleman would, on his return, contribute special articles to the Press on tho question generally. Mr. David Smith spoke strongly in favour of the Gothen- burg scheme, and Messrs. Thomas J. Holt, Samuel M. remperley,and Thomas Cooke against. Mc.Key replied, after which the meeting closed. COLLIER'S BLACK BLENDED TEA. 20. per quarter lb.,Advt

div.head: EAMLESTOWN AND NEWTON
div.p: EAMLESTOWN AND NEWTON

GUY FAWKE'S DAY, There is plenty of evidence in this district that the old custom of celebrating the plot of Guy Fawkes and his conft derates, is falling into decay. On Monday, several fires were to be seen blazing in various parts of the district, but the display of fireworks was remarkably meagre, and fell very far short of the displays of ether years. No accidents in connection with the event have been reported.

div.head: EARLESTOWN DISTRICT SCHOOL.
div.p: EARLESTOWN DISTRICT SCHOOL.

We would draw attention to the advertisement on the front page of a children's concert,to be given in the Town llall, Earlestown, on Thursday even- ing next, by the scholars attending the Earlestown district school. In addition to the vocal and instru- mental items, there will be a short operetta entitled "Fairy Fay," and judging from the time and labour spent in training the youngsters, the entertainment should be well worth a visit. About five o'clock on Tuesday morning a fire was discovered in an out-building, behind the Millstone Inn, Newton, occupied by Mr. Webster. The build- ing contained a number of fowls, joiners tools, and other things, all of which were destroyed. A supply of water was obtained from Messrs. Gillispie and Mason's paper mill opposite, but the building was practically gutted before the fire was extinguished. Considerable damage, estimated at about £2OO, was done.

div.head: ACCIDENTS AT THE VIADUCT WORK'S.
div.p: ACCIDENTS AT THE VIADUCT WORK'S.

On Tuesday morning a youth named H. Themes employed at a cutting machine, at the Viaduct Works, got his hand entangled in the cog wheels of the machine, with the result that two of his fingers were torn off. He was taken to the surgery of Dr. liandyside, where his injuries were attended to. —On Wednesday afternoon a man named Frank Lowe, employed in the spring shop, was lifting a large spring from a pile of other springs, when the whole pile fell on his left leg. He received "first aid," by the works ambulance men, and was after- wards removed home. Dr. alentineatteuded and found he had sustained a compound fracture of the left leg.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLADY.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLADY.

The weekly session of the Ebenezer Lodge of Good Templars was held on Tuesday evening in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown. Bro. W. J. Taylor presided and there was a good attendance of members and visitors. One candidate was admitted to membership. Bro. J. Singleton, L.D., read the digest of No. 1 convention to be held at Vulcan on Saturday next, after which the reports of the officers were submitted and adopted. The election of officers then took place and they were installed by Bro. J. Singleton, L.D., assisted by Bro. Sparks of Warrington and Bro. Armstrong of Hope of Earlestown. The various Committees were then appointed after which the Lodge was closed in due form by'Bro. A. Morris, C.T.
" OUR NEEDLEWORK GUILD."-SOUTH LANCASHIRE DISTRICT.

The annual exhibition of clothing made by the members and associates of the above guild, was held in the Town Hall, Newton, on Friday after- noon. The exhibition was opened by Mrs. - the president, who delivered a short address eic- plaining the objects of the guild, and appealing for assistance. There was a very poor attendance of the general public, but there was a numerous di,.- play of useful articles of clothing, suitable for all seasons and purposes. At the close of the exhibi- tion the clothing was despatched to various parishes for distribution among poor and deserving people, and to several charitable_institutioas in the district.

CONCERT AT EARLESTOWN. A most successful concert from a musical point of view was given in the Town Hall, Earlestown, on Tn sday evening, in aid of liquidating the debt on the Welsh Congregational chapel. There was a very fair audience, who had the pleasure of enjoy- ing a programme of songs rendered in a most effici- ent oni artistic manner. The artistes, were principally from St. Helens, and their various contributions were well received. The concert should have opened with a trio "Turn on, old time," ' but owing to the late arrival of Mr. J. H. Thomas (bass) it had to be held over, and the programme opened with a cleverly executed " Rondo " on the violin, by Master Jackson, a very youthful per- former. Miss Roberts, a powerful soprano, followed him with that beautiful song "Alone on the raft," which she sang in a perfectly finished style, receiv- ing an encore for her pains, "The stars of Normandy" received equally efficient treatment at her hands. Mr. Harry Berry. the well-known tenor, was quite at home with the song "The last watch," and he was heartily applauded. For his capital rendering of "Let me like a soldier fall," he was recalled and sang" My desert star." He also gave a beautiful interpretation of "The Holy City." The song Tit for Tat" was fairly well sung by Miss Rosa Reefe, and for the song ".Our wedding bells' she received an encore, but did not respond. The song "Oh, oh, hear the wild winds blow" was capitally treated by Mr. J. H. Thomas, who has a powerful bass voice, but his efforts did not receive the appreciation they deserved, he also gave an efficient interpretation of the song "Thy sentinel am I." The duet " Excelsior "was ably handled by Mr. Berry and Mr. Thomas and was duly appreci- ated, and Master Jackson was applauded for his violin execution of " Carmeen." Mr. Wilson Black- ledge supplied the humour, his contributions caus- ing much merriment.

div.head: DEATH .OF A NOTED RUNCORN
div.p: DEATH .OF A NOTED RUNCORN
FOOTBALLER.

MILITARY FUNERAL. The sad death occurred very suddenly on Satur- day at noon of Mr. John Lewis, 34 years of age, of 15, Ellesmere-street, Runcorn. He became ill whilst conversing with Mr. Robert Wright and Mr. Gatirratt in the Market Place, and went to the door of the Market Superintendent's office. Mr. Garratt, noticing his condition, supported him, and sent for a medical man. Shortly afterwards he died, before the arrival of a doctor, and was conveyed an an ambulance to his home. He had been in ill health for several months,and unable to work. Dr. Robinson who had attended him, certified the cause of death to be the breaking of,a blood vessel. Some years ago,Mr. Lewis was a prominent "for ward" in the team of the Runcorn Rugby Football Club, ' .and had also gained several medals and other prizes !or bowling. He was, further, a member of the G. Company of Runcorn Volurateers. He leaves a widow and one child. On Wednesday afternoon, in the midst of a drizzling rain,the remains of the deceased volunteer were interred in the Runcorn Cemetery. The funeral procession was joined by the Bind of the Runcorn Volunteers, in com- mand of bandmaster .Outhwaite, et, firing party of thir- teen privates, under Sergeant Woodland, whilst the rear was brought up be several other volunteers with Dr. Preston (chaplain) and Captain G. F. Ashton Representatives were also present from the Run- corn Football Club, and the Star of Freedom Lodge of the Grand United Order of Oddfellows. On the -coffin, which was carried by volunteers, were placed the helmet and accoutrements belong- ing to the deceased. At the Cemetery were several hundreds of spectators. Dr. Preston, who is chaplain to the detactment, conducted the funeral cere- mony. The deceased during his lifetime, had been very popular in the town, and at the graveside there were many mourners who were utterly unable to restrain their grief. The sight was a most impressive one, ex- pressions of sorrow being general. After the ceremony the hand. accompanied by the Volunteers returned to the Drill Hall.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 01, 1894.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 01, 1894.
WESTON.

THR FORTHCOMING BAZAAR.—By referring to OM advertising columns it will be seen that on the 14th oi this month and the three succeeding days a grand bazaar will he held in the Runcorn Public Hall. the object is to procure sufficient money to build a church in the township of Weston. This is a village with a population of 1,300, yet it does not possess a church, divine service having at the present titne to be conducted in the National tichools. It is hardly necessary to remark that there is not sufficient accommodation for the congregation, consequent; a great effort is being made by almost everyone in the village, as well as many residents in Runcorn to raise the necessary funds. The bazaar, which will be on a very large scale, will represent " Runcorn in ye Olden Tytne," by means of specially painted scenery and model houses of Old English design, specially built for the occasion. Ladies dressed in costumes of the Cavalier and Round- head period, will superintend the stalls, and there will be all kinds of entertainments. On the first day it will opened by the High Sheriff of Cheshire, on the second by Lady Brooke, on the third by Master Brooke, and on the fourth and last day bY Mr. Eustace Carey. The prices of •admission are within the reach of all, and it is anticipated that the event will prove the medium of securing a good round sum in aid of the proposed , church.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT EARLESTOWN. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

The dark nights and mornings are with us, but lam sorry to say that the Commissioners or their servants do not seem to have recognised this Cact. The cry of more light has already been raised, and not without some reason. [ will give the authorities the credit of lighting the lamps early enough in the evening, but they take good care to see that they are extinguished early enough too, in fact very often too early, the consequence being that any belated individual who finds himself returning home after half-past ten, has often to be content with the scant light afforded by the stars, if there happen to be any about, but just lately they have been conspicuous by their absence. it was only the other night, I met the official whose duty it is to extinguish the lights, actually turning them out before 10-30, and there was no moon shining. It is bad enough to be left without light in the even- ing, but I fancy the workingmen who have to turn out at 5-30 on a winter's morning, will suffer very great inconvenience because of the want of light. I understood there was an order given by the Com- missioners that certain lamps were to be left lighted all night, so that workingmPn might be able to find their way to work in a morning without danger. If there is such an order it is not being carried out and I think some steps should .be taken to see that the matter is attended to.

A big noise is being made around these parts just now with regard to "common rights "; the particu- lar place alluded to being Newton Common. To use a hackneyed phrase, " in the memory of the oldest inhabitant," Newton Common. has always been a common, over which the public have been allowed to roam without let or hindrance. In late years, however, it is a notorious fact that small portions of the common have been enclosed, no; all at once, but piecemeal. Nothing has been said, and now on one particular portion a number of houses have been erected. If the land is common land, and as such belongs to the people, this is filching with a ven- geance. But this is uotall. Not content with tak- ing over one side of the common, it has been pro- posed to build houses on the opposite side, plans of which have been deposited with the Commissioners. 'Being- the representatives of the people the Com- missioners very properly refused to pass the plans until an incontestable right to the land was estab- lished, and accordingly they have left this matter over for the new District Council to take in hand. I hope that they will be able to prove that the common belongs to the people, and that no man is at liberty to 'enclose it at his pleasure.

Until about 12 months ago there was another tract of waste land called the Menses, over which the public could roam at will. Now,some portions of it have been enclosed and cultivated, and other portions are being gradually fenced in., until very soon it will be completely enclosed, and probably we shall see a notice stuck up warning people that they are trespassers. Of course somebody may be within their rights in doing this, but I should like to know, and I daresay many others would,whether the Menses is considered as common land.

Meetings have been held in the various wards in connection with the District Councils election, and candidates to represent the wards have been selected. The "candidates catechism" has been answered, and I should fancy pretty well ex- hausted, but what strikes me as rather peculiar, is the fact that a divergence of opinion amongst the several candidates is conspicuous. Would you be- lieve, that out of the whole 13t, only one candidate, and that a workingman, had the courage to say that he was in favour of a School Board.

_ On other points the repetition of the answers bid fair to become monotonous, and I fancy I am not alone in hoping that the next few weeks preceeding the election will furnish us with some form of excitement. Of course the whole. rround will have to be gone over B,E,Yain, only I hope the matter dealt with will not be of such a stereotyped form. There are many things, besides common rights and pci.v- ing, want looking into of much more interest and importance to the township.
MYSTERIOUS DEATH AT ST. HELENS
A HUSBAND'S IDENTITY. STRANGE EVIDENCE.

An inquest was held by Mr. Brighouse at St. Helens, on Wednesday, concerning the death of Mary Chesney, 76 years of age, wife of John Chesney, labourer, of Chorlev, who was found drowsed in the canal late on Saturday night.—The Coroner, addressing the jury, said there were some remarkable circumstances in connection with the case. Just before the woman's death a man was seen in her company, and the man was seen about the spot after her disappearance. Three St. Helens per- sons had identified the husband as the man wile was seen in her company, and if that were true it would be a suspicious circumstance. Chief Constable Wood had ' made inquiries of the Chorley police, and Inspector Steel had been over to that town making inquiries. As a re- sult it was perfectly clear that the ()wham] was not in St. Helens on Saturday night, and he could not be the man who was seen in the woman's eompany.— Chief-constahle Wood said he had not the slightest suspicion respecting the husband. the Chorley police haying informed him that Chesney was at home in bed at nine o'clock on Saturday night.—lnspector Steel said he saw seven persons at Conpull and Chorley, who all positively swofe that the man Chesney was at home on Saturday afternoon and night.—John Chesney,labourer, ot Chorley, hut at present working at Coppull, deposed that the body was that of his wife. The last time he saw her alive was on Saturday week, when she came to visit some friends at St. Helens. He emphatically denied seeing his wife on Saturday night. Ho WWI not in St. Helens on that day.—Margaret McDormet.nf Canal-ha,nk East, said the woman stayed at her linuse last week. She. always spoke well of her husband. She was expecting him over on Saturday night and went out to -meet him—W. M'Coomb, foreman of the Globe Chemical Works, spoke to the diecnvery of the he ty ia the water on Saturday night. —Police-constable Whalley said that half an hour before the body was discovered he saw the woman Chesney and a man, in Atlas-street, Parr, about 200 yards from the spot ve:n.te her body was afterwards found. They were walking in the direction of the canal. He certtinly thought the axoman's husband (now in court) was the man who was with her on Saturday night.—The Coroner : They say ,we all have our "doubles" in the world. I have not seen mine- yet. (Laughter.) He asked whether the various witnesses had accidentally identified Chesney. Chief-constable Wood said when Police-constable Whal- ley saw Chesney in the Police Court he at once identi- fied him as the man he had seen with Mrs. Chesney. He then sent for Mrs. Sprowson who corroborated him. —Mary Sprowson, wife of W. Sprowson, of 154, Merton Bank-road, was next put into the box, and said she had no doubt that Chesney was the man she had seen with Mrs. Chestier on Saturday night...—ln answer to the , coroner as to the possibility of Chesney being able to get from Chorley and hack on Saturday night, Chief-con- stable Wood said-there was a train from Chr rlPy at seven o'clock, arriving in St. Helens at eight o'clock. There was one back to Wigan at 9 mei Little, 98, Mer- ton-road, said at 9.10 on Saturday night he saw what to the best of his belief, was Chesney, now in court, at the canal bank. He had the same clothes on, and was so fiutte'el he mild hardly sneak at first. At last he said " Which is the way in Smithy-brow." He (witness) toll him, and when the woman had been tiiken out of the canal he said "0 Lord, I cannot face that dead body." Chesney was like the man in every shape and form. The Coroner : This man has a peculiar voice? Witness: His voice is the same too.—The Coroner: It is very remarkable, to say the least of it.—Witness: He was dressed just as he is now exactly, but he seemed to he in beer.—The Coroner: The whole thing is unsatisfactnrr. These witnesses have nothing t.l gain or loose in this affair.—Dr. Fred Knowles gave evidence to the effect that he had made a post-mortem examination, but found no marks of violence on the body.—The Coroner said he understood that Chesney had a third witness : if so he had better call him.—David Boustnn, a fellow workman with Chesney,said he had tea with the latter on Saturday evening, and he never left the house from half-past, six until Sunday morning. Chesney wont to bed at half-past seven n'cloek.—The jury returned an open verdict of "Found drowned," which:the coroner Snid would not prevent the police from taking any further action they thought fit if they got any further evide nee.

M. GLADSTON E AND RELIGIOUS EDUCATION.

Mr. Gladstone has written a letter to a clerical friend who had asked his advice how he should vote in the London School Board election. The right hon. gentle- man says that in his opinion an undenominational system of religion framed by or under the authority of the State is a moral monster. The state has no charter from Heaven buch as may belong to the Church or to the individual conscience. It would, he thinks, be better for the State to limit itself to giving secular instruction than rashly to adventure upon such a system.
LECTURE AT THE: aINCORN LIBERAL
CLUB.

At the Runcorn Liberal Club on Thursday night the winter session was opened by the delivery of a lecture entitled "Common bands and common rights," the lecturer being the well-known Mr. W. H. Chadwick, of Manchester. Mr. Clarke, chairman of the committee presided, in the absence of Mr. Philip Speakman, C.C. Mr. Chadwick deslt exhaustively with his subject, pointing out how lands had come into the possession of the aristocracy, and that in thousands of cases if lords of manors were asked to prove their right to certain lands they would be totally unable to do so. Thousands of acres had been 'fraudulently enclosed, and many of the so-called owners of property at present had no existing proof of their right to it which would be satisfactory in a court cf law providing the judges were strictly honest. In relation to "common rights," this question hard been very much neglected in England up to the present time but thanks to the Local Government Bill, which had been carried by a Liberal Government, with Mr. Glad- stone at its head—(applause)--Parish Councils would be able to take the matter up, and if the proper men were elected on the Parish Councils a large amount of the land, which would otherwise be claimed by the lord of the manor, would he set apart for the recreation of commoners. This should prove an important question at the coming elections, and the electors should net omit to ask their candidates if they were prepared to take up the question of Common lands and cam mon rights."—At the conclusion a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Chadwick. Mr. W. Handley supported the motion, and said that Mr. Brunner had presented their Library with Mr. Shaw Lefevre's latest work on " Commons and common land," which book couid now be borrowed by any member. Not only had Mr. Brunner done this, but he had felt so strongly on the question that he had engaged a barrister specially to look up the matter so that in all probability he (Mr. Brunner) might draw up a Bill for introduction into Parliament which might make it easier for the people in England to get the land. He thought they had some 70 or 80 acres still unenclosed in Runcorn, and possibly, in the near future, this land might be converted into a park for the people. (Hear, hear, and applause). A survey of this common land was still in the Commis- sioners Board room. He also thought that the question was a yery necessary one to put to the candidates for election on the various councils. Subsequently the chairman was given a hearty vote of thanks and the meeting ended.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT WARRING- TON.

The sth of November has come and gone! This year's anniversary has not been particularised by any special event. No organised exhibitions have been held but the private shows seem to have been as popular as ever. From 7tolo at night the sky was alive with squibs,rockets and other pyrotechnic displays while the air resounded with the reports of cannons, crackers, bombs, Szc. Bonfires, too, were in strong evidence, and a stranger might reasonably have thought that the country was in the hands of a ruthless invader, judging by the "lurid lights" which could be seen through the darkness in all directions. Accidents seem, luckily, to have been at a discount. As far as I know not a single casualty of a serious nature has been recorded. -- The recent wet and stormy weather has been largely grumbled at,but, like other things, it has its redeeming features. Latchford people especially have reason to be thankful, for the previous inky and evil-smelling condition of the canal has given place to a. light brown colour for the water as well as a greatly increased freshness of the atmosphere In other words the great sewer has been "flushed," and the people round about are correspondingly thankful.

The humorous evening held at the Y.M.C.A. on Wednesday night did not belie, its name for laughter was the order of the day—or, shall I say, evening. Mr. Ashton, as humorous ewertainor, excelled himself on this occasion with his well- chosen selections from Mark Twain. Artemus Ward, and Max Adder. There was a very large attend- ance,!and altogether the affair was a signal success. The musical portion of the evening WWI well sus- tained by the different ladies and gentlemen who had tendered their services.

That the Warrington people have not lost their love of music was clearly evident to those who attended Mr. R. H. Pearson's concert in the Gym- nasium of Tuesday night. The concert, was a suc- cess in every way, in fact, it might almost be said that. the audience got two concerts for their money as an encore was demanded and accorded for every selection. An excellent. quartette was provided in the shape of the four vocal attistes who must cer- tainly have been flattered by the outburst of enthu- siastic applause which greeted every song. Miss Niabel Chaplin as lad y-'cellist was an unparalleled success, bPr clever and expressive interpretations of the most difficult pieces being received with every expression of pleasure by the audience. The build- ing is not very well adapted to concert pnrposes, owing to its defective acoustic properties ; still, considering the tight place in which concert- givers are flxed,it, made a very good substitute and presented a pleasing appparance..
THE WARRINCiTON LICENSING
APPEALS.
THE SWAN LICENSE REFUSED.

The appeal of the tenant, Mr. John Merry Beacon, and the owner, Mr. R. Dobson, of the Swan Inn, against the decision of the Warrington magistrates refusing the renewal of the license was heard at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions on Saturday. Sir W. B. Forwood presided, and the other magistrates on the Bench were Messrs. R. Holt Ecimundson (Golborne), Richard Kelly, Thomas Evans, E. Can- nington. C. W. Goodison, James Lister, and Thomas Snape, MP. Mr. Mulholland, instructed by Mr. R. Dobson, junr., appeared for the appellants, and Mr. Horridge, instructed by Messrs. Lewis Davis,Liver- pool, as agents for Mr, H. B. White, magistrates' clerk, represented the respondent justices. Mr. Horridge, in opening the case for the respondents, remarked that the grounds upon which the license was opposed were nearly all the grounds upon which a license could be opposed. First with regard to the wants of the neighbourhood, the Bench had had before it a plan of this district in the Pelican case, , and the Swan Inn was close to the Pelican Inn. He 1 had a similar plan showing that the Swan was the centre of a congested area in Warrington, I and the house was not required by the wants of the neighbourhood. The next and the great point had regard to the construction of the budding. He did not hesitate to submit that no B,nch would license such a place now-a-days. It had no entrance to Bridge-st. in a sense, the entrance to the house being up a narrow passage 3ft. ein. wide. He submitted for the inspection of the Bench photographs showing the house and its approaches,whith he briefly described. With regard to the doors at the entrance to the passages, it was said by the other side that they were never shut, hut the doors were there, and if shut the house was completely cut off from. the street. Mr. Horridge mentioned that there were convictiens againAt the house, the last one being in December last for serving two p,Aicemen with drink ' while on duty, the magistrates fining the then tenant £5 and endorsing the license. .

Mr. Thomas Cook, architect and surveyor, Liverpool, produced a plan which showed the number of public- houses in this particular district and in the town. There were a '(neat number of houses round the Swan Inn. He had made an enlarged block plan showing the position of the premises, and the tw& doors by which access was gained.

The Chairman: Arm these all c .vered passages? Witness said they were, and if tne doors ;were closed there was no approa,h to the house. Front Bridge-street to the house was 52 feet. He described the court in which the house was situated. There was a flight of stairs lead- ing from the court into the upper premises of a drapers' shop. There was also a urinal under the back window of the shop. The window of the bar parlour opened on to another court.

Cross-examined by Mr. Mulholland.—He was not !a, resident of Warrington and could not say anything about the management of theS wan or whether the doors were opened or shut. The doors could be easily removed. The house was not a place easily inspected by the police. Re-examined by Mr. Horridge.—The house was en- tirely surrounded by property, and could not be brought into the front street. The steps in the court led to Mr. , Dobson's premises and not to Bailey's. There was noth- log' to prevent beer being handed out of the bar parlour window to anyone in the G_ lit outside. Mr. Horridge put in the co. viction recorded against the house in December last, this Loncluding the case for the respondents. _ _

Mr. Mulholland said that in 1893, the former landlord,. Cheadle, gave notice to leave the premises, but in December, two months afterwards, and when presum- ably he might be careless in the management of the house, and when certainly the landlord could do no more than had been done to get rid of him, he was convicted of giving drink to policemen, the circumstances being of a most peculiar kind. This was the only charge . recent times it was possible to make up against this house. Mr. Beacon was now the tenant, and there was no objection whatever to him. With all the fierce light which had lately beaten upon Warrington public-house, not one word of censure could be passed upon the con- duct of the house by the present tenant. Mr. William Owen, J.P. , F.R.1.R.A., said he attended at the licensing ses.3ions in 1893 and remembered the re- port of the Chief Constable. All the licences were re- newed subject to alterations hein,g made as required. He had 38 houses in his own hands. A committee went through the houses. There were no undue facilities for drinking at the Swan. It was a very comfortatqle house. The passage past th.-- house was a thoroughfare. He had gone through it for many years. He had only heard of the doors being closed once on the occasion of a fire. There should he no difficulty in the way of police super- vision. The passage was used by the public as a short cut from Bridge-street to Upper Bank-street, and Buttermarket-street.
Cross:ex3mined by Mr. Florridge : fie did not suggest that the public house could be brought to the front strmer.

Mr. S. Hunt. the Chief Constable, said he had known the Swan Inn 31 years. The present tenant was a man of most exeellent charact7r. The offenus, of the last tenant, Cheadle,was that of -serving two policemen when on duty. They had been served by a barmaid, but it was saidthe landlord saw it through a door. There was no difficulty in supervising the house when they got at it. The police patrolled the passage. He had never served any objection against the house. The passage was used a public thoroughfare. It relieved the font traffic from Bridge-s. to Buttermarket-st. He thought the urinal might be hnproved.

Cross-examined by Dr. Thomas, who acted for Mr. Horridge for a few moments his absence : He did not think a house situated as this was. would be licensed in these days. Mr. R. Dobson, solicitor, slid he was the son of the owner. After the magistrate; appointed the committee in 1893, he waited upon it and asked if the tnagistrates had any objection to raise to the Swan or any sugges- tions to make. Dr. Thomas objected to this'evidence being gone into. The Chairman said the Beach only wanted to get at the truth. - -

Mr. Dobgon said hat fli undertakin,g was asked for in the case of the Swan. Wien wked if the committee had any suggestions to make, 0 ey replied they had nothing to sly. Ills father wi I prepared to make any alter- Wions they might mg,' re. Cross-examined by Dr. Thomas : The magistrates who r‘fused the license were Warrington magistrates. Per- hips they knew the requirements of the town and per- haps they did not. Councillor Dr. Cannell said he knew the Swan Inn, where Mr. Beacon did a large off-business. It was a free holm.. He thought the license ought to he renewed. There were very few free houses in Warrington. He considered the accommodation excellent and the sanita- tion good. No one could come out of the house without being seen from Bridge-street.

Mr. W. Walker, architect and surveyor, said he knew the Swam very well. He thought it conveniently situ- ated fcr a public-house. II; was one of the few free houses, and he thought that was a good reason the license should be renewed. Cross-examined by Dr. Thomas: He preferred to go to this house for Burton beer than having to drink some of the beer they got in Warrington. Mr. Fletcher said he was stepson to Mr. Dobson, the owner. He had a draper's shop in Bridge-st. He often went to the Swan Inn for tea, and he considered the house a very convenient one. • Mr. John Gerrard, hairdresser, said he found the Swan Inn very convenient, and he should like to see the license renewed. Mr. James Atkinson. manager for Mr. Dobson in his drapery business, said there was nothing objectionable in his opinion to the passage leading to the house. Mr. J. M. Beacon said he had hen tenant of the Swan since the 2nd July. He had found the business a good one, and it was incrasing,. He had a seven days' license, but he did not open on Sunday. He had beautified the house since he became the tenant. He had a seven years' lease, and the house was not tied. Mr. Cook had been through it and was much struck with the ace .immodation. Mr. nes, chemist., said he had lived in this neigh- , bourl- )(1 nine years and used the Swan. He was in faro, j -if the license being renewed. l'iilrdennings, painter and decorator, Manchester-road, said he had gone to the Swan Inn since Mr.lleacon went , there, An d found the house a great convenience. _ _

Mr. Horridge drew the attention of the Bench to some remarks of Mr. Justice Wills to the effect that he thought it was the deliberate iniention of Parliament that the liability for a conviction should not be got rid of by the expedient of transferring the license to a man of respectable character. Mr. Hunt himself had said that the premises would not be licensed now-a-days. They could not get rid of the objections in this res- pect.

RE-OPENING OF THE VIADLTCT INSTI- TUTE LIBRARY, EARLESTOWN.

Many of our readers will hail with satisfaction. the announcement given on our front page, that the Library at the Viaduct Institute which has been, closed since February last,will be re-opened for the issue of books on Monday evening next,at the usual time, seven o'clock. It may doubtless be asked why the. library has been closed for such a length of time, and inquiries in this direction may beset at rest by the simple answers—for the preparation of a catalogue. Some few years ago, owing to the very large addition made to the number of books then comprised in the library, it was found absolutely necessary to enlarge it, by extending the building then in existence, and providing extra space for several thousands of books. Since that time some hundreds of books have been added, but the catalogue then in force, was to all intents and purposes obselete,because it did not contain anything like a full list of the books which could be obtained at. the Library. ! This was a decided disadvantage to a reader, who was. wholly at a loss to know what books were obtainable.. ! The Committee fully recognised the injustice, if it may !be so termed, of this, to borrowers, but when it is con- sidered that the library contained something like 4,400 volumes, the magnitude of the task of preparing a com- plete and exhaustive catalogue will be apparent. There was, however, no other way out of the difficulty, and during the time the library has been closed,e: Ormand, the secretary of the institute, with the assistance of the librarian, Mr.Banton, has been engaged in re-organising the library, and compiling a complete and comprehen- . sive catalogue of the books contained therein. We have been favoured with an advanced copy, and a perusal of it leads us to the conclusion that its comoreheasiveness is so complete, and the arrangement so simple, that any schoolboy or girl with ordinary intelligence will be able to tell at a single glance whether the hook he or she re- quires is in the library. The catalogue is classified in six parts—theology and philosophy ; history, biography; voyages, and travels ; poetry and the drama; law, science, art, and technology ; miscellaneous literature, fiction—each part bearing a distinctive letter. The com- pilation is carried out something on the lines of a dic- tionary, with this difference, that if the reader requires • a book by a given author, the title of which he has ~ foreotten, he has simply to turn to that author's name, ' and ha will at once see whether such a book is included. , Again, if a reader does not understand the meaning of a r title, Hot only is the title given, but it is interpreted i below in plain English. Another unique feature in this ~ exhaustive work, is a list of the nom-do-plumes of : authors, with their real names. The classification is at ._ once perfect and complete, and comprises in itself not only a catalogue, but a fund of information not easily : obtainable. The catalogue, as stated, can be obtained , from the librarian, and if readers are wise they will do well to secure one. Of course it will be understood • that the library is open to the public, whether members of the Institute or not, upon payment of certain sub- scriptions, for instance, if it is required to borrow one volume at a time.eaclelibrary night,the terms are for one year Bs., if two volumes at a time 9s. 6d. per year, and !so on in something like the same ratio, up to four volumes at a time.

TIrE PArusu COUNCILS ACT EXPLAINED —ln the Town Hall, Frodsharn, on Friday evening, a meeting was held by the Progressive Party of the village with a view to having explanatory addresses on the above Act. There . was a large attendance of the general pubic, Mr. T. A. Rigby presiding. After the Chairman had given an address, relative to the Act, and its effect chiefly upon village life. Mr. Roger Bate, C.C., (Tarporley) and Dr. Hodgson, C.C., (Crewe) gave expositions of the measure. Mr. Bate confined himself te District Councils, whilst Dr. Hodgson dealt with Parish Councils. At the conclusion questions were asked and satisfactorily answered. On the preposition of Mr. Guest, seconded by Mr. .1. M. Williams, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Rigby and Dr. HodgsQn for their addresses. Subse- quently a similar compliment was paid to the Chairman on the motion of the Rev. J. Renton, seconded by Dr. Uedgson. The meeting then closed. Nannow ESCAPE —Shortly after half .past seven o'clock on Saturday morning a porter at Helsby Railway Sta- tion, named William Ellanis, experienced a narrow es- cape. Having detached some carriages on one line, he was stepping from behind them when he was knocked down by the train which travels between Ditton and Helsby. He fell inte the four-foot way, and the whole train passed ever him. When picked up it wila found that his head had been severely injured by theft:T.-box of the engine scraping it, hut beyond this and the shock there was no injury. It is very fortunate that the per- manent way is low just where the man was knocked down, or he would certainly have been killed outright. He has been medically attended, and is reported to be progressing favourably towards recovery..

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES

ROTTEN RABBITS. On Monday at the Borough Police Court ,Robert Leigh, Teel's Curt, Town Hill, was charged with offering for sale on the 30th of October. eight rabbits which were unfit for human food. Defendant pleaded guilty. In- spector Powell said that on Tuesday last he was in Lil- ford-st. when he came across the defendant, who had some dead rabbits for sale. On being asked how he was 'selling them the defendant said "from 100. to 1. each." The inspector examined them and found that they were wholly decomposed and stinking. He took them to the Town Hall where they were inspected by Dr. Gornall and Mr. Wm. Owen. Mr. Powell had been conducted by the defendant to a house where he had sold another rabbit and this was also found to be in a state of decom- position.—Defendant stated that he did not know that the rabbits were unfit for human food and as this ap- peared probable the magistrates let him off with a fine of ss.

A RESULT OF THE BAD TRADE. A striking example of the prevailing difficulty to ob- tain work was witnessed at the 11rough Police Court, on Wednesday morning. A poorly-clad man named James Hill, was charged with running away from the borough of Warrington and leaving his wife and four children chargeable to the common fund of the Warring- ton Union since the 25th July last. Defendant pleaded not guilty. Mr.B. Shearer, relieving officer, stated that on the 25th July the defendant's wife and four children, aged 12, 11, 3, and six months, respectively, were ad-: mitted to the Workhouse, defendant having left the town. She remained with them 15 weeks at a cost of £l7. Be not having turned up, a warrant was issued , for the defendant's arrest, an I he was apprehended on ' Tuesday.—Defendant stated to the magistrates that he bad left his wife at the time named by a tacit agreement to seek work, he being a clog„ger by trade, but was also able to turn his hand to the iron trade. For the whole four months he had been wandering up and down the north of England, but had not been able to get work once during that time. He had written to his wife once while he was away, but had received no answer. He had no intention of defrauding the Guardians, and was not aware that he should keep in touch with Nlr.Shearer. The magistrates considering that there were several ex- tenuating circumstances, and Mr. Shearer not wishing to press the case, adjourned it for a month.

r, CRUELTY TO A. HORSE.—Jonathan Pilling, Antrobus-st., Was charged with having on the 17th inst illtreated, abused and tortured a horse by travelling the same in an unfit state. Inspector Luff, R.S.P.C.A., stated that on the night of the date named he was in Winwick-street, when he saw the defendant driving a horse attached to a greengrocer's cart, which had fastened behind it an old grey mare. It was excessively lame on both fore legs. It was .uffering, from ringbone and the legs had been doubly blistered. The defendant told him that he had bought the animal at Stretton and was going to take At to a knackers-yard in Manchester. It was totally unfit to be travelled. Defendant stated that he paid 15s. lor the animal with bridle, cellar, etc., attached. He bought it for the knackers. He was fined 53. including Costs. A DANGEROUS HUSBAND.—John Moores was summoned by his wife, Hannah Moores, for using threats towards her on the 16h September.—Complainant stated that between 10 and 11 o'clock on the night of the day men- tioned she heard loud knocking at her shop door. Her daughter and herself were in bed at the time, and the former on going to the window, found that it was her father (the defendant) below. Complainant who had been separated from her husband for twelve months on account of his cruelty towards her, went downstairs and fetched a constable t ) remove defendant. When theotficer arrived however, defendant had secreted himself in an adjoining outbuildingo nd as soon as he had gone he went to the back premises of complainant and tried to get into the house. He threatened complainant and said that the next time he came would bring a six-chambered revolver for her. Complainant concluded by saying that she had eight children, and during the last twelve months the , defendant had not given her a penny for maintenance. She managed to keep herselrand her children by carrying on a little shop, and the defendant by his conduct was driving the custom away from it.—Defendant denied that he had deserted his wife, but was ready to live with her and to support her.—He was eventually bound over to keep the peace towards his wife for six mnnths, himself in a surety of £lO, and two further sun-ties of £5 each. div.head: ALLEGED STABBING AFFRAY AT
div.p: ALLEGED STABBING AFFRAY AT
WARRINGTON.
QUARREL BETWEEN BROTHERS.

On Monday morning, at the Borough Police Court, before Mr. F. Monks, chairman, and other magistrates, Thomas Troy, Berry's-yard, was charged with having on Saturday, the 3rd inst., unlawfully wounded John Troy, his brother, by stab- bing him with a knife in Winwick-st.—Mr. Hunt (chief constable) stated that the complainant, John Troy was A labourer, and lived with his mother at 8, Berry's-yard. The prisoner would also like to live there, but owing to his had habits the rest of the family would not have him there. It appeared that the complainant was drink- ing on the night in question in the Bay Horse, Winwick- st., together with a man named Mooney. He left the snuggery and was going out when he was met by the prisoner who asked him for some money which the com- plainant refused to give him, whereupon the defendant laid hold of him and John had to push him to make him let him go. De- fendant then went out and called the complainant to follow him and on doing so the two had another scuffle on the ground in the midst of which John called out "I am stabbed ! I am stabbed ! " On his rising Mooney and another man saw the blood running down complainant's face and after taking him to a druggist who could not dress the wounds, they took him to the infirmary where it was found that he was cut in four places about the face. Meanwhile the defendant ran away but was ultimately arrested by Detective Sergeant Monaghan.—John Troy, the complainant who appeared with his face traversed by strips of plaister, corrobor- ated the Chief Constable's statements. He said that when struggling on the gound outside the public-house, he suddenly felt something sharp in his face and called out as above. He then became uncans.;ious and remem- bered nothing till he was taken to the infirmary. He had several times heard the prisoner say that he would " knife " him.—Henry La.nr.,dale,junior house surgeon at the infirmary said that John Troy was brought to him at 9-30 on Saturday night last. He was suffering from four clean cut wounds on the face. The principal one was near the right ear and 1 inches long and of an inch deep. The other wounds were one,one inch long and the same depth and another an inch long near the nose and the other was under the left eye and was one inch long and the same depth as the others In hi opinion the wounds were caused by some sharp instrument but they were not of themselves, very dangerous. He dressed the complainant's face and found that he had lost a large amount of blood.— Patrick Mooney, Berry's-yard also gave corroborative evidence.—D.S. Monaghan deposed to apprehending the prisoner about 11.30 on Sunday morning. Witness told the prisoner that he wanted him for stabbing his brother on Saturday night. Prisoner replied "I was going to give myself up after half-past twelve." Monaghan brought him to the police station and charged him in the usual manner to which the prisoner said "We were, in the Bay Horse Inn and he hit me twice. We went outside and both fell down and he kicked me. I stabbed him to defend myself, and threw the knife away." Monaghan had not been able to find the knife. The prisoner pleaded net guilty. Complainant denied ever striking the prisoner or kicking him but admitted giving him a push to make him let go. The prisoner was com- mitted to take his trial at the Liverpool Assizes.

div.head: COUNCILLORS ROBERTS AND SHAW,
div.p: COUNCILLORS ROBERTS AND SHAW,

APOLOGY FOR ASSAULT BY THE LATTER. At the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday morning, before Mr. F. Monks in the chair and other magistrates, Mr. Forshaw (Davies and Forshaw) appeared in the case of Councillor H. Roberts, J.P., and Councillor W. J. Shaw for an assault committed on the former by the latter after the last Council meeting. His client (Mr. Roberts) had, Mr. For- shaw said, taken out a summons for assault, but the magistrates would not now have the trouble of hearing the case, as Mr. Shaw had apologised to Mr Roberts, undertaking not to repeat the offence and tl pay all the expenses incurred. That apology was to be published in the three local papers. Under these circumstances, his client would, with the per- mission of the Bench, withdraw the summons. This was accordingly agreed to. Mr. Shaw did not appear.

div.head: BOMB OUTRAGE [N LONDON.
div.p: BOMB OUTRAGE [N LONDON.

About midnight on Sunday a bomb was exploded in front of the house of Mr. Reginald Brett, in Tilney-st., Park-lane, London. Mrs. Brett had just entered the house from her carriage, but although the hall door and windows, as well as the windows of neightmuring houses, were shattered she escaped injury. Colonel Majendie has taken possession of the fragments of the bomb. Mr. Justice Hawkins lives at an adjacent house, and this fact Causes the opinion to be entertained that his Lord- ship was intended to be the victim of the outrage, and that the perpetrators of the crime are Anarchists. A Colonel Majendie, after an examination of the frag- ments gathered at the scene of the explosion on Sunday night in Mayfair, is of opinion that the bomb was made on the principle of the one found on Polti, the anarchist who was convicted at the Old Bailey a few months ago.
