RUGBY. WARRINGTON v. LANCASTER. These two teams met on Saturday at Lancaster to fulfil the first of their two annual engagements. It is a very singular circumstance that no matter how well Warrington have been playing previ,us to ineetin,z Lan- caster, they never do themselves juqice when they go to John o' Gaunt's old town. Thera must surely bc

something in the air which disagre?s with the team. They have not won a single match there for the past four years, and still they always account for them quite comfortably at Warrington. Lancashire have not been doing so well this season, and as Warrington have been improving recently, it was generally thought that there was a good cllance of breaking the ill-luck which dogged Warrington's footsteps, but they were unable to do so, and sti'l another defeat has to be chronicled. Had the referee given his decision differently on an occasion when Burton got over the line, which will be related helow.the result would most probably have been a much more favourable one to Warrington. The Warrington ta in were so disgusted with the decision that they never played with any vigour at all to the end of the game, and Lan- caster were not slow to take advantage. Trio rain came , down in torrents when the team arrived in Lancaster, and a nfiserable game was looked forward to, but Mr. , Underwood's good luck in always having fine weather to perform his duties of referee was not broken, and when the time of kicking-off arrived, it was beautifully fine. The teams who did battle with each other were as fol- lows :—Warrington: Full back, Boscow ; threequarter- backs, Carey, Cunningham. Heesom, and Burton ; half backs, J. T. Bate, and Clark ; forwards, Turner, Thorni- ley, Berry, Taylor, Bailey, Savage, Andrews, and Houghton. Lancaster : Full hack, Cowan ; three- quarters, Bleasdale, Fawcett, Wilman, and T. Gibson ; half backs, Lambert and Gardner; forwards, Carter, C. Gibson, Pinch, Stephenson, C. Thompson,Satterthwaite, Winder and Wilson. In the first half Warrington had to face the sun which was very dazzling at the time. Stephenson kicked off, and so well did Lancaster follow up • that Bosco w was called very early to defend.

Warrineton for a time sent Lancaster to the right about, but a kick by Gardner to half way was forther supple- mented by a forward rash, and tascow pulled Lambert up when almost across the line. Burton paid a similar compliment to Wilman immediately after- wards. Gardner now had a tun on his own account, and was knocked into touch on the line. From the line out, the hall was sent over but Boseow touched down. Lancaster again returned to the attack, and a passing movement between the home halves was spoiled by a forward pass. An exciting struggle now ensued in the visitors' quarters, and just as Burton appeared to be getting clear away, a knock forward spoiled the chance. From the ensuing scrim- mage, Lancaster took play to the line, and another minor fell to the homesters. The kick out was met by Fawcett, who was loudly applauded for a fine run through his opponens, but Boscow brought him to grief. The ball was at length got over again, and a race for possession took place between Gibson and Boscow, which ended in favour of the latter, and another touch down was the result. Carey was prominent immediately afterwards by spoiling a series of passes between the Lancaster backs. Up to now, the home team had done the greater portion of the pressing, bit a grand kick by Boscow, transferred play to the opposite end. This advantage was nullified, by Lambert accepting a pan for Bleasdale, and racing more than half the length of the field. A • dribble by Bailey, Savage, Turner and Taylor took play into home quarters again, and a penalty kick was ' awarded Warrington in a favourable •position, for off- side play of the home halves. Burton took the hickebut for once, he was unsuccessful, and Fawcett securing the ball commenced a series of passing, but was not stopped until Ileesom and Boscow stepped in. The efforts of Lancaster were at length rewarded by Lambert scoring a capital try, which Gibson however, was not able to improve. there was nothing worthy of comment from now to half-time, which found Lancaster leading by a try to nil. After the usual exchanges, after the interval, War- rington settled down for a time in the home 25, but a cembined rush gave Lancaster the advantage, and a struggle ensued near the Warrington line. It was at this point that an incident occurred, which completely spoiled the game, and robbed it of all interest. The bail becoming loose for a scrimmage,Burton quickly gathered it up, and dodging one player after the other, he left them all behind, and after a run three-quarters the length of the field, he got over, and grounded. A Lan- caster player was coming at top speed, and Burton after placing the ball on the ground dodged his opponent. From some reason or other, the ball bounced up, either from Burton catching it with his foot, or else from the force with which it was placed on the ground, and jle referee thereupon said that it had not been placed, and would only award a minor. This aroused such disgust amongst the Warrington players that for a time the game was suspended,and after it was restarted, they appeared to have lost all interest in the game, and (-rely played in a half-hearted fashion. The decision was most unjust, for Burton Imied that he had bounced the hall as the referee contended that he had. This was a sorry ending indeed to one of the most brilliant runs that has taken place for a long time. The game from now to the finish was not call for much comment. War- rington were defending the greater portion of the time. The game was however of a scrambling nature. At length Fawcett rushed to the corner, and Burton And he went down together taking the corner flag with them. The ball was grounded just over the line, and Lancaster thus gained their second try, which Gibson failed to improve. Thompson made his mark from the drop out, and Gibson had another attempt at goal again failing. The ball went over the line, again, soon afterwards, and Wilson :grounded just as Burton reached it. Gibson was successful with the place this time. Full time came soon afterwards, when Lancaster were declared victors by one goal, three tries, to nil. This decisive result was without doubt due to the decision of Mr. Underwood as the players played very carelessly indeed afterwards,and allowed the Lancaster men to take advantage of. them. The referee's decision was the suhject of much adverse critisism even by many Lancastrians. WARRINGTON A V. LANCASTER A.

There was a fair attendance on the Wilderspool en- closure on Saturday afternoon to witness the match be- tween the above-mentioned teams. The Warrington combination had been considerably weakened owing to the drafting of several players into the first team for the engagement at Lancaster. Soon after three o'clock the ball was set in motion, the Warrington men playing with the sue in their faces during the first hail. The home team at once forced their way into the visitors' territory and a number of scrimmages took place near the visitors' geal line. Nothing Came of the effort,how- ever, and the visitors transferred play to the Warring- ton quarters. Give and take play followed until Lan- caster had an opportunity for scoring but they failed to take advantage of it. Warrington now played up with vigour and placed the visitors on the defensi ve,Warring- ton's opportuniy for scoring came soon afterwards for they were awarded a free kick in a favourable position, for off-side play on the part of one of the visitors. Lawless took the kick and was successful in placing a fine goal. The whistle for half-time soon afterwards sounded with Warrington leading by a goal to nil. Even play for some time followed the restart. Warrington were granted another free kick owing to off- side play by the visitors but the kick was a failure. The home team again pressed their opponents and Forster receiving a pass from Moores raced over the line, scoring a try. Lawleet took the place kick and scored a goal. This was followed shortly afterwards by Sanders for Warrington scoring a try, and a goal was again kicked by Lawless. Near the call of time Lancaster were awarded a free kick and essayed at goal, hut failed. Nothing further was scored by either side and the game ended in a victory for War- rington by three goals to nil. The following composed the teams : Warrington : full back, Manninn ; three- quarter barks, Moore. Lawless, Edelsten and Gleave ; half backs, Foster and Foden ; forwards, Thornton, San- ders, Barratt, Hampson, Hughes, Knight, Borrows, and Fairhurst. Lancaster: full back, Hartley ; three- quarters, Cardwell, Wilson, Leake and Young; half- backs, Lexham and Sandham ; forepards, Atkinson. Baent, Bond, Matthews, Herbert, B. Thompson, Sharpe and Harrison. WELLFIELD-STREET RANGERS V. FROGHALL JUNIORS.— A match was played between Wellfield-street Rangers and Frngliall Juniors and ended in a draw with no score, each getting one miner. WARRINGTON EXCELSIORS V. FAILSWORTH A "TEAM. —Played at Bramall-green enclosure on Saturday, before a good attendance. Owing to the recent rains the ground was in a sloppy condition. The visitors won the toss, and elected to play downhill. At the call of time the Failsworth teans had won by two goals (one penalty) one try to one try, or eleven points to three. WARRINGTON Sr. PETER'S V. WARRINGTON RANGERS (2ND).—This match was played on the ground of the latter. Some good passing on the part of the Saints' backs resulted in Hughes getting over, Holnrook making, a poor attempt at goal. Half-time arrived with the score—Saints one try, Rangers nil. On the restart Flolbrools passed to Price, who outran Camp- bell and scored at the corner, Faster making a good attempt at goal. Shortly afterwards Price ran in a try, the goal-kick failing. Time was called with the score— Warrington St. Peter's, three tries; Warrington Rangers, nil. STOCKTON HEATH V. STANDISH SOUTH END.—Th.QP tea frR met at Standish on Saturday. Standish kicked off, and the usual preliminary scrimmages took place in the Stockton Heath 25. Barber relieved. and Standish again rushed the ball down to the Stockton Heath lines, but the splendid defence of the Stockton Heath hacks Prevented any scoring. From a scrimmage in his own 25 Barber secured an opponent's pass, ang eluding all opposition scored a magnificent try behind the poste,the kick at eoal failing. Lally and Smith got the ball away splendidly, and transferring, tc Cross the latter player male a splendid run to the hnmesters' lines and trans- ferred to Broady,svho made a dash for a try,but slipped

near the line. From a throw-out Higham made a splen- 7 did attempt to score, but was prevented from ground- ing the ball,and a minor resulted. The drop-out brought about half time, which found St, ckton Heath leading by a try to nil. Stockton He ith re-started, and at once pressed. Webster secured and passed to Barber,but the latter player was ruled back for some indefinite reason. Smith broke away and passed to Broady, who had the misfortune to knock on when a try was at his mercy. Cross now essayed a drop at goal, which was charged down, and Webster saved the ensuing rush in fine style. Standish now broke away. but Hamblett was always safe and returned to touch finely. Standish made a des- perate effort to escape defeat and pressed for some time, but could not break through the delence, La,llv especi- ally saving wonderfully. lime was now called, and Stockton Heath won a splendidly-contested game by one try to nil. Stockton Heath are to be complimented for being the .first to defeat Standish South End this sea- son. The forwards combined splendidly, and the way they held the much heavier weight of the home forwards was a treat to witness. The backs played in their usual brilliant style, Barber especially playing a finished gam. WARRINGTON ST. MARY'S V. LOSTOCK.—This match was played on the Liverpool-road ground on Saturday. F. Hampson turned out for his old club. Owing to the late arrival of the visitors the captains decided to play two 255. Lostock won the toss and elected to play with the wind. From a scrimmage rligginbottom came away, passed to O'Brien, he to Rutter, who threaded his way through his opponents and scored, Hampson failing to convert. Play continued to be of an even character, and nothing more was scored up to half time. After the opening exchanges the Saints again invaded the visit- tors' quarters,and a round of passing by the home backs gave Pendlebury trouble, who again managed to clear, but Warburton after a tricky run got in at the corner. Thomas failed. On resuming Roua,hley kicked well to centre, and Higginbottom rounded his oopnents in grand style and scored under the posts. W. Roughley failed. Re-starting Warrington accepted a pass from Hampson and added his second try. From this point the Saints had it all their own way,Hamoson an.l Edgar adding a try each, and when the whistle sounded time the Saints had added another win to their unbeaten re- cord, winning by six tries to nil. PENIEVI V. VIDNES PARISH CHURCH'. —Thi;4 match was played at, Widnes on Saturday. Widnes kicked off and even play followed, W. Parson scored for the visi- tors after ten minutes play. Shortly afterwards Chad- wick equalised with a low shot. Tne visitors pressed for a while and from a free kick Bowyer headed through Singleton adding another directly afterwards. The home team was penalised and Singleton scored a grand goal, half time being reached with the score, Penketh 4 goals, Parish Chureh 1 goal. After a scramble in front of the vis;tors goal the home team scored. Play was mostly in the visitors quarters the homesters by combined rushes added two more goals final score : Penketh four goals ; Widnes Parish Church four goals. The Penketh Team was :—Ef. Bowyer (goal). W. Higham and A. Dykes (Backs), W. Whitfield J. Fligham, J. Warburton (half backs), J. Davies-,J. Bowyer, H. Singleton, (forwards.) W.Parson, N. Parson, and

At half-time the score stood one goal to none in favour of the visitors. On resuming, the play was even and the game was hotly contested. Bason got possession of the ball and scored another point for the School after a fine run. The final score was :—Lymm Grammar School. two goals; Warrington Reserve, one. ALL SAINTS V. PARISH CHURCH.—PIayed OR the ground of the latter. The Saints kicked off, and after ton minutes' play Muckley scored. After the restart Parish equalised after a bit of exciting play in front of the visitors' goal. Muckley added another for the Saints before half time. In the second half the Saints pressed Continually, Gandy, Muckley, and Hall adding one each. The game ended in a win for the Saints by six goals to one.

ST. PAUL', RESERVE V. WARRINGTON RA ISIBLERS.— This match was placed on the ground of the former. The visitors kicked off with their wind in their favour, play became settled in the visitors' half for ten minutes from the start, and from a combined rush of the home forwards. HOLY TRINITY V. ORFORD.—This match was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday last In beautiful weather. Trinity having to get two substitutes. In the second half the visitors played for all they were worth and succeeded in scoring four goals, S. Mather (2) T. Rigby and E. Rigby being the scorers. The homesters
several times became dangerous but the visitors' backs played a good game and managed to keep them from scoring and at call of time the score stood—St. Mary's 4 goa!s, Viinwick 2 goals,__

THE PARISH COUNCILS A.CT.
PAPER BY MR. J. C. SUTTON.

There was a well-attended meeting in the Wes- I leyan Schoolroom Penketh,ou Thursday evening last to hear Mr. J. C. Sutton, C.C., clerk to the Warring- ton Board of Guardians read a paper on the Parish Councils Bill. Mr. C. E. Parker occupied the chair and amongst others present were :—Messrs. R. Garnett, J.P., W. Houghton, S. Sutton, J. Milling- ton, W. Rath bone, E. Cross, W. Aitken, A. White, H. Cartwright, B. Hobson, John Newcombe, It. Cooke, John Atherton, J. Mainley, W. Taylor, W. Furness, J. Dignum, J. France, J. C. Routledge, W. Walters E. W. Clarke, J. Jackson, J. Watson, and J. Wright The CHAIRMAN said they were there that night to have explained to them the recently passed Parish Council Act. He thought it was one of the most pleasing features in our Engiish national character that as soon as any measure became law, whatever party happened to be in power,they at once recognised that law as being the -expression of the national will and loyally sought, to obey it and carry it out. So they had met that night that they might learn how to carry that law into effect. He trusted that the interest they manifested in that parish council bill woull be sustained and that the meetings in that parish would be more largely attended. (Applause.) Mr. J. C. SUTTON, in the course of his paper, said the Local Government Act contained 89 sections, many of them elaborate and many sub-sections. It repealed provisions in 26 other Acts of Parlia- ment, it made reference to or incorporated more or less all the parts of 40 other statutes. The theory f.f the Act was to induce people to take a deeper interest in their local government. Let them use their best efforts to avoid legal pitfalls and their best intelligence, free from their common prejudices, in the exercise of the privileges that were conferred upon them. They would find that the Act made complete severance of property and property interests from representation. Let them then by tnis "one man one vote" principle make the election of their future councillors from reasons of their fitness and intelligence. (Hear, hear.) Let them not deny to any of such men their support because of their opinions upon subjects that were wholly discon- nected with the duties appertaining to their office. (Applause.) They found from the Act that the ancient alliance hitherto existing between the duties of church- warden and overseer was completely severed, that the first retained his powers and authority upon Church affairs and that the, second was to be the officer of the Council for the discharge of purely parochial work. The word parish originally meant the district of a priest.

might be exercised by the parish meetings subject how- exer as to some things to the approval of the County Council. The parish meeting might appoint committees. The election of parish councillors would proceed on or before November 24-th, and the overseers would publish notice of the parish meeting for Tuesday, December 4th, not earlier than six p.m. Mr. Sutton then dealt at length with the mode of procedure at the meeting, and pro- ceeded to explain the matters which the Council had power to take in hand stating that they might provide a parochial office, parish books, parish chest, fire engine, five escape, &c., and they would have charge of parish property, village greens, allotments—whether for recreation or for gardens—make representation as to unhealthy dwellings or obstructive buildings under the Housing of the Working Classes Act, 1893. The meet- in.. could adopt any of the following acts:—Lighting and Watching Act 1833, Baths and Waslahouses Acts 1846 to 1882, Burial Acts, 1852 to 1885, Public Improve- ment Act 1860, and Public Libraries Act 1892.

At the conclusion ef the reading of the paper a num- ber of questions were asked by the Chairman, and Messrs. Furne-gs, J. Di;;;num, A. White and Appleton. Mr. Sutton answered the questions satisfactorily. Re- ferring to a question put by the Chairman as to the position they would be in at Penketh, regarding the Re- creation Ground, Mr. Sutton said he was afraid it wasa question of law. With regard to questions of that kind he would always be glad to put a question to the Local Government Board. He felt sure that he would get a reply. A question was asked as to whether 6J. in the 2 was the limit of expense. Mr. Sutton said 3d. in the 2 was the limit,but by gett rig the permission of the County Council they might go to GI in the 2. That did not apply to the adoptive Acts which were quite independent of the 6d. limit. Before the adoptive Acts could be taken advantage of they must be approved of at the parish meeting. If a person objected he could demand a poll. In reply to another question Mr. Sutton said he did not think that the parish council would have power to lease land and relet it to any work- man who mig,'t desire it. In regard to the question " Will the parish council have the right to deal exclu- sively with common land?" Mr. Sutton said the Coun- cil would do so where no right existed in any person. A vote of thanks was passed to him on the motion of Mr. Dignum, seconded by Mr. R. Garnett, J.P. A similar , compliment was accorded the Caairman, and the meet- ing terminated.
THING 3 HEARD AND SEEN AT WARRINGTON.

The ill-feeling which has been simmering in the Town Council for some time has at last come to a head, in the shape of a physical-assault upon Coun- cillor H. Roberts by Councillor W. J. Shaw. The assault complained of by Mr. Roberts was com- mitted after the ordinary business of the last Coun- cil meeting had been disposed of when some remark made by Councillor Roberts led his irritable brother councillor to make an unwarrantable attack upon him, using threats the while Mr. Roberts immediately setaliated by taking out a summons for assault against Councillor Shaw and on Monday morning at the Police Court Mr. F..,rshaw, solicitor briefly stated to the magistrates that as Councillor Shaw ha i apologised for the offence the action, would not be proceeded with. To make a public apology to be published in the three local papers must be a bitter pill for Councillor Shaw to swal- low. In addition to this it will be no extra gratifica- tion to have to pay all the expenses incurred,which lam told, will amount to about £s—rather a high price to pay for his little indiscretion. Looking at the matter from another point of view, Councillor Roberts has certainly acted for the public good in bringing the affair into full publicity. It is quite. clear that the town cannot afford to have its affairs decided by fisticuffs rather than by discussion and, argument.

It was a sad death, that of the man Granger who, died at the Infirmary on Friciay last week through being scalded in a vat at Dallam-lane Brewery. But, as will be seen from the report of the inquest,, the firm of Messrs. Walker and Son were entirely exonerated from Name by the jury. The unfor— tunate man has left a widow and children, but it is satisfactory to learn that the firm, although not liable for the accident, have decided to contribute, 20s. weekly to the widow for three years.

There have been numerous addresses given in., various parts of the country to explain the working of the new Parish Councils Bill, and Warrington: and district has in no way been neglected. In this district, however, the orators have been content with explanations by word of mouth, but I notice that Mr. Pletcher, the clerk to the Northwich Board: of Guardians, in the course of an address upon the subject at Oakmere, went further, and conducted a mock election. He sent round nomination papers, with names upon them, and the whole parapher- nalia in connection with an election was gone. through. This is an original way of "doing the thing," and would do more to explain the matter than an hour's address.

Just a word about the licensing appeals. I con- fess I cannot imagine by what method of calcula- tion it is made out that the county magistrates are superior to the borough magistrates. I cannot see why the appeal against the borough magistrates' decision should be taken to the no less irresponsible county magistrates. Surely if an appeal is made, it should be made to more responsible persons than country squires, of which the majority of county benches are composed. Magistrates for the borough are as capable in every wa3 to decide upon these matters, as their so-called superiors. A great out- cry has been made about the borough bench being "packed," and that decisions are given in accord- ance with the opinions of the magistrates, and not from the evidence. But the same thing might be said with regard to the Quarter Sessions, and I heard several persons interested in the case say that it all depended upon the composition of the bench whether the appeal was granted or not. In hearing election petitions, the case is heard before two judges, and I am sure that if the same were the case with licensing appeals, there would be much more satisfaction than appealing from one bench of magistrates to another.
THE SHIP CANAL.
THE CANAL AND THE COTTON TRADE.

A largely attended and representative meeting of cotton spinners, cottsn merchants, and cotton brokers was held in the Victoria Arcade, Manchester, on Tuesday, to make arrangements for the formation of a Manchester Cotton Association and the establishment of a cotton market in the city. Mr. C. W. Macara (President of the Cotton Spinners' Federation) presided, and speeches M support of the scheme were made by Mr. W. H. Hol- land, M.P., Sir Joseph Leigh, M.P., Mr. Alderman Emmott (Oldham), and others. Resolutions in favour both of the establishment of a cotton market and the formation of a Cotton Association were unanimously adopted, and a provisional committee, compilsing a large number of influential merchants and manufacturers was appointed to take the necessary steps. Mr. J. N• Bythell (Chairman of the Ship Canal Company) made all announcement which the meeting received with loud cheers. He stated that the Ship Canal Company had been trying for some time past to make arrangements for the direct shipping of Bombay piece goods from Manchester. That morning he had received a telegraT saying that a tender made under the Company auspices for the shipment of all piece goods from Man- chester to Bomtay for two years from the Ist JanuarY next had been accepted. This, he added, was an earnest of what was to come.

div.head: TWO DIFFERENT FORMS OF GOVERNMENT
div.p: TWO DIFFERENT FORMS OF GOVERNMENT

would exist in the parishes. Ina parish such as Cuerdley with a population below 300,a parish meeting under one chairman would,with the overseers, exercise powers cor- responding to those of Parish Councils. In other parishes such as Penketh and Sankey the parish meeting and the parish councils would rule. The county government included the County Council, borough Corporation,rural district councils, parish councils, and parish meetiry4s. There would also be the Boards of Guardians, overseers, and in many places, as in the Warrington Union for three years, Highway Boards. The duties of the High- way Boards would afterwards be taken over by the rural district councils. The work and iesponsibilities would assuredly increase and they would be brought face to ' face with new and greater expenses that would involve , heavier rates. (Hear, hear.) It was ever even so, as might be seen by tracing the progress of local govern- meet. The

div.head: BOARD OF GUARDIANS
div.p: BOARD OF GUARDIANS

in the Warrington Union would under the new Bill con- sist of one guardian for each ward in each urban parish (Warrington, Newton, and Haydock) and a district councillor for each rural parish. The Assess- ment and School Attendance Committees would be appointed from the Board. County magistrates were no longer ex-officio guardians neither were they qualified. to serve on c.inmittees as such. The Board might ap- point a chairman, vice-chairman, and two other mem- bers from the list of persons qualified to be guardians. The qualification of a guardian in a borough was being on the electoral list or having resided in the year pre- ceding nomination in the Union or being qualified for election as a Councillor. The usual disqualifications as bankruptcy, paid office, interest in contracts, &c., pre- vailed. A widow, or a married woman or a spinster might be elected a guardian if qualified as above-m-n- -tioned. The election was by ballot, each elector giving but one vote—there would be neither plural nor property votes. In that Union all guardians and district council- lors would after election continue in office until April 15th, 1898. A notice would be issued on December Ist of the election of rural district councillors for rural parishes and of election of guardians for Union wards. Forms of nomination might he obtained free of charge either from overseers or at his (Mr. Sutton's)office. Such nominations duly filled up must be delivered at his office not later than December sth at 2 p.m. Notice of the persons nominated and of his (Mr. Sutton's) decisions upon validity would be published on Decenaher 7th. Nominated candidates might withdraw in writing not later than 4. p.m. on that day. If a poll was necessary, notice of the 'poll to be taken be- tween 12 at noon and 8 p.m. on Monday, December 17th would be published on December 11th. The elected Guardians would elme into office on Friday, December 28. In that Union the, rural Guardians had hitherto all been elected members of the Rural Sanitary Authority hereafter all

div.head: RURAL DISTRICT COUNCILLORS
div.p: RURAL DISTRICT COUNCILLORS

would be Guardians. The rural sanitary district would be governed by a rural district council consisting of a chairman and councillors. The councillors were to be qualified and elected in like manner as Guardians and for the same term. Any person qualified to be a Guar- dian for a Union comprising the district was qualified to be a district councillor for the district. A rural district council might elect a chairman from outside the council. The chairman would be a county magistrate during the period of his office. The County Council had consider- able powers in respect of the grouping or of the dividing ot parishes into wards and in respect of increasing the number of district councillors. The elections were by ballot, and the powers of the district council were in some respects extended. With regard to

URBAN DISTRICT COUNCILS the borough was not interfered with. The Commission- ers of Newton and the Local Board of Ha.vdock would be the urban district councils for those districts. They would take over existing duties, powers, and liabilities and they had further powers conferred on them. Their qualification, disqualification and mode of election cor- rosponded to that of the Guardians. 'They retired in thirds annually, according to their position on the poll. With the sanction of the County Council they might retire simultaneously in each third year. They would he elected by ballot upon the same dates and at the same pelliug stations as the Guardians. They might appoint overseers and the assistant overseer with the approval of the Local Government Board,and would have the powers of the vestry and powers under the Poor Rate. Assess- ment and Collection Act, 1869. They' might enforce the direct payment of rates by all occupiers. In rural parishes that were without a Parish Council the parish meeting would

APPOINT OVERSEERS. In other rural parishes the parish council woul appoint overseers. In urban districts and boroughs an order of the Local Government Board would be required to enable the councils to appoint overseers. Overseers would he appointed on April 15 or within seven days from that date, and their appointment must be reported forthwith to the Clerk of the Guardians. If within three weeks that official did not receive such a report then the Guardians would appoint overseers and their appointment would prevail. An overseer was still in the words of the 43rd of Elizabeth to be a substantial householder. Churchwardens ceased to act as overseers. The legal interest in property vested in the overseers or in the churchwardens, except property connected with the church or an ecclesiastical charity would be vested n the Parish Council. The duties of overseers were narrowed to the making of valuation lists, the making and collection of rates and duties connected with electo- ral and jury lists.

div.head: PARISH MEETINGS.
div.p: PARISH MEETINGS.

In that Union two parishes Cuerdley and Houghton, having populations below 300 would have no parish council. The population in both cases being over 100, it either township desired, the County Council would con- sent to the election of a parish council. When the population of a parish was below 100 the County Council might or might not consent to a parish council according to circumstances. The County Council would group such parishes with adjacent parishes if desired. At Cuerdley and Houghton the Parish would meet annually in March and „.would then appoint a chairman for the year. They wou d also ap- p,,,ia overseers. The chairman and overseers would be la body corporate carrying out the decisions of the parish meeting. November 611 :—" We, the members of the Warrington and District Hairdressers Association,wish to state publicly that we instituted, carried out,and paid for, the recent prosecution of hairdressers for Sunday work for the purpose of safe-guarding our hours of labour, and, further, had Councillor Shaw sought in- formation respecting the matter before mentioning it at the Town Council meeting, he would not have made such a stupid blunder as he did on that occasion. div.head: NEWTON DISTRICT COUNCIL ELECTION.
div.p: NEWTON DISTRICT COUNCIL ELECTION.

Sir,—There are so many questions being put to the , District Council Candidates which are eliciting an inter- eating variety of answers that there seems a probability of the one question of paramount moment being some- what overshadowed and obscured by minor issues. I allude of course to working men councillors, and the absolute vital necessity of the Council meetings being held during the evening. I venture to bring this matter forward because of the open hostility of two candidates—Dr. Handyside and Mr. Smith—and the uncertain utterances of other; re- garding evening meetings. To Mr. Emmett's credit be it said that he stands forward as the workingman's champion, and that if a working man should be elected on the Council he would be agreeable to meet in the evening. Taking Wigan as a centre, there are, it is said, sixty working men candidates, within a radius of seven miles. It behoves every work- ingman elector who values the privileges which have now been conferred upon him to give his loyal support to these candidates,and where he finds the ranks of wealth and position closing up to exclude these workingmen he Should let it be seen that he regards such a movement with ciAtestation. A spirit of emancipation to workingmen breathes through every page of the Act and inspires every line, and if workingmen electors will be true to themselves and do their duty they will see that no man is elected to the Council who declines to pledge himself to meet in the evening. This meeting after business hours with the ratepayers as an audience—as provided by the Act— should be one of the chief factors in awakening and sustaining an abiding interest in all our local aff airs.— Yours truly,
ELECTOR.

THE IRON TRADE. Sir,—We see from the local papers that Mr. Carson, of the White Cross Works, movqd the following resolution at the British Iron Trade Association,held at Glasgow,and it was unanimously carried :—" That this meeting being convinced that it is desirable that the workingmen em- ployed in connection with the iron and steel industries of this country should have a more full and accurate knowledge of the foreign competition and the serious prospects of their trades, is of opinion that copies of the various reports and papers, showing the extent and character of foreign competition, should be circulated a'monrst the various unions representative of working- men employed in metallurgical industries." Now, sir, I ina7 say for myself and for the iron workers in this dis- trict, we would hail with much pleasure any such in- formation on the question of foreign compPtition. But let the subject be fairly dealt with. Let us have the cost of royalties per ton on iron in Germany and in England, and the difference between railway and shipping rates, and the cost of directorship at home and abroad. I think when that is done—and not till then—will it be fair to compare the English workman's wage with that of the foreigner. And lam forced to believe that by a reduction of tariffs and royalties to the cmntinental level there would be no fear from foreign competition, and that England would bold her own with any nation in the world.—Yours truly,
T. MALKIN.

MORE LIGHT UPON THE "SEED PROBLEM.' Sir,—ln fulfilment of a pr-nnise made in your columns in the spring, and believing your then correspon- dents upon this subject to be anxious to come at the truth, I wish to record the results of some experiments I made to test this question : Is it necessary that a seed, or part thereof, should die to germinate and produce a perfect plant. To this and I dissected the germ or embryo from many grains of wheat and grew them suc- cessfully—while the remainder of the seed remained— and still remains—unchanged. Now, sir, J. D. Hooker, in his " Primer of Botany "—editorially endorsed by Professors Huxley, Roscoe, and Palfour Stewart—says the seed consists of two parts—a dead part and a living part, the embryo. Well ! even the most extravagant commentator—and I have noted some—hesitates to say that the germ dies and is revived. No ! it is the dead part which these gentlemen are determined to slay ! Now, the question hinges very much upon the definition as to what constitutes vegetal life and vegetal death. A plant to be truly said to he living must possess at least two of these three powers—assimilation, growth, and re- production. Wheat flour possesses none of these powers, loss of which would constitute death. In other words that which never was alive cannot die. One would think this a self-evident proposition ; but the blindest are they who won't see. It would be interesting to see what " Ben Chayill " has to say to this ; and it may be inter- esting, to your summary correspondent, Felix Summers, to learn that there is an embryo in wheat before quicken- ing, and that this can be grown separately irom the seed. —Yours &c.,
JOHN PEERS.
HISTORY AND MYSTERY OF A GREAT FRAUD.

Sir,—ln my last communication the two exploded ideas of medicine, which have, in their explosion, des- troyed the dogma of medical infallibility, were" venesec- tion and inoculation" not " vivesection." About the year 1777 Edward Jenner, a youth, ap- prenticed to Mr. Sudbury, surgeon at Berkeley, heard a woman insisting that she could not have the smallpox because she had had the cowpox. In 1793 the same Jenner published this cowpox affection as a protection from smallpox after 30 years industrious and pains- taking inquiry and experiment" according to Dr. Baron. This industry consisted of occasionally mentioning the superstition—which was common to all the Enelish dairy counties, and had been so before Jenner's time, at certain local medical convivial meetings. Here he was nooh-poohed and confronted with scores of cases in which smallpox had occurred after cowpox contracted by Milking diseased cows. Jenner himself saw many such cases, according to his champion, Dr. James Moore. With all the will in the world to " make a name," Jenner dare not publish the superstition in the face of such overwhelming testimony. Meantime, the Rev. bar. Drew, Jesty and Dr. Naish, both taught and practised the inoculation of cowpox as a protection against smallpox ; while Jenner slumbered others were working. He spent his leisure in writing a comic natu- ral history of the cuckno,which procured him the letters F.R.S. It was not until May, 1796, the first actual experiment was tried by him. He took matter from Sarah NAmes' sore hand and vaccinated John Phipps with it. In July

the boy was inoculated with smallpox with only local effects. On the strength of this solitary experiment, Jenner wrote a paper and sent it to the Royal Society, whose council returned it as too good for them. Note not one experiment direct from the cow or horse had been tried when Jenner attempted to foist his immature discovery on the faculty. In the Spring of 1793 the cowpox re-appeared owing to the prevailing, rain having made the horses' heels sore. A boy was vaccinated from a man's sore hand con- tracted frorn horsegrease. (Tile boy in abut a month tok fever and died). Three other men who had caught horse grease were inoculated with smallpox ; all resisted the contagion. One afterwards caught smallpox casu- ally and died. . With those few unsatisfactory experi- ments Jenner issued his epoch-making paper which he called "An inquiry into the Variolae Vaccinae, &c." By the title the whole question was very astutely begged. Variolae vaccinae —smallpox of the cow. Why if this new (?) disease is the C9W'S Mail-PDX it must protect from all future smallpox. Everyone knew, or thought he did, that the sanv, person could not have the smallpox twice. All the best men opp Kied the new practice : Birch, Brown, Mosely, Goldson, and Ingen- housz. Besides the lymph propagated by Jenner was soon found to leave erysipelas and phoyedenic ulcers be- hind. Happily his lymph was exhausted and Woodville and Pearson discovered some spontaneous cowpox in London (which Jenner expressly declared to be spurious). They practised vaccination at the smallpox hospital where—on Jenner's autho- itv—tho patients caught smallpox concurrently with vaccinia, and consequently had pustular eruptions and would not take smallpox on subsequent inoculation. Jenner was supplied with this contamin- ated lymph with which he renewed his own experiments. This smalipoxed cowpox will account for much of the temporary prophylaxy of the early vaccinations—the patients had really had smallpox and not the vaccine disease. In " some further observations" Jenner further traced the genuine cowpox as that which arose from the horse's greasy heel.

Dr. James Moore, Jenner's right hand man, wrote : "All persons after passing through vaccinia are for the remainder of their lives unsusceptible, to smallpox." 1800. Dr. Ring and 32 principal medical men in London, signed a testimonial to Jenner, declaring " the vaccin- ated are perfectly secure from smallpox." Then Dr. Simon, of the Local Government Board, sass " the vac- cinated are safe from smallpox because they have had it." All modern candid inquirers (e.e.. Prof. Cruikshank and Dr. Charles Creighton) say the variolous test was unfair and not decisive; but the disasters reported immediately on all hands were sufficient to enlighten, and did enlighten, all impartial men. The eminent men already named, judged vaccination by its fruits. All our history has come fr,lns Jennerls vacciaa- tors—we submit the following as Poi-nothing, more fav- ourable to vaccination than the reality. Ist. It is a fact Jenner's son was inoculated with smallpox when brought within reach of danger—although Ise hail been cowpoxed by his father before. The Hon. R. Grcsvenor, vaccin- ated by Jenner, took smallpox cc severely that everyone despaired of his life. Med. and ?hrs. Journal, 1801, re- ports erysipelas and phyoedenic ulcers after vaccination. Royal College Surgeons, 1807, report scrofula as a conse- quence of vaccination also 56 cases of smallpox includ- ing three deaths. Medical Obs. 1808, gave 535 cases after vaccination 97 deaths. Of the first 20 vaccinated at Geneva 17 took smallpox and three died. James Moore reports two deaths from vaccination and three from smallpox after vaccination. Dr. Willan records 50 cases 1800-1806. In Warrington, Kendrick reports 16 cases after vaccination, giving no reaction with small- pox inocculation—all caught smallpox casually. One died eleven months after vaccination. Another case within six months. in Prescott (Myers reports) one died 18 months after vaccination. la Liaerpool a child died of the worst kind of confluent smallpox three years after vaccination (McCartney), and another died of con- fluent after good vaccination (Fleetwood). I have two other cases in 1801, after being vaccinated six and ten months respectively, and many for all periods from six months up to five and ten years which all happened before 1806. I shall be glad to furnish anyone with particulars. These are, sir, a few only of the failures which even at the time led all wise men to refuse to receive the filthy rite and which surely demand a re trial now. I am prspared to discuss the matter from the modern stand- point if any medicus dare champion the foul and loath- some practice.—Yours sincerely, BIBLIOTHEQUE. Runcorn, Oct. 31st, 1894.

div.p: MR. R H. PEARSON'S CONCERT.

Mr. R. H. Pe,arson'a grand concert in the War- , rington Gymnasium on Tuesday evening opened the musical season in the town so fittingly and with such eclat, as to make it almost too much to expect that the interest thus shown at the com- mencement can, under present. adverse circum- stances, continue through the winter. The want of a building suitable for concerts on this scale will, during this season, be keenly felt, and the still incomplete state of the new Public Hall must inevitably damp much enterprise in concert-giving amongst local musical bodies. But, in spite of all difficulties Mr. Pearson scored a brilliant success in the concert of Tuesday last. Such accommodation as the Gymnasium affords was taken full advan- tage of by the numerous and fashionable audience assembled to listen to the performances of a concert party comprising artistes, some of whose names are familiar as household words. Madame Clara Samuel( as eoprano,MissJeanie Rankin as contralto, Mr. Henry Piercy and Mr. I). Ffrangcon-Davies as tenor and ,bass respectively, form a vocal quartet of such excellence that no doubt could be felt as to the enthusiasm which would characterize their reception. Miss Mabel Chaplin as a violoncellist,and Mr. Philip Cathie as a violinist, are probab:y both unknown to Warrington audiences, hut it is only due to say that such eminent soloists as both , proved themselves to be, are always welcomed and accorded rapt attention. The lady-'cellist received quite an ovation,•and this is not surprising when her power to move an audience by a most expres- sive style and charm of manner, has been expe- rienced. The finished performance of Popper's "Romance," and "Vita," and ITollman's exacting fantasia on airs from "Carmen," fully attested Miss Chaplin's skill and command of technique, and a discriminating audience gave unmistakeable evi- dence of its hearty appreciation of her efforts. It was clearly manifest that Mr. Philip Cathie was suffering from indisposition, and this fact no doubt accounted for the absence of much of that energy and verve which he mny be expected to show under normal conditions. Ile was nevertheless able to impart. a rich pathos to the vocal adaptation "Light," of Ffandel's Largo which Miss Rankin sang with feeling, and to which the violinist played an obligato. Madame Clara Saratiell and Miss Jeanie Rankin had each one song, at least, in the programme which was really worthy of their powers. " The scent of the and Asthore " are superior settings of verses of more than ordinary interest, and the vocalisation of both shewed how thoroughly the singers had caught and become imbued with, the sentiment and the intention of author and composer alike. Encores followed as a matter of course, and the" Robin Adair "and " Genevieve "respectively still further delighted the audience. Mr. Henry Piercy.soffered more than his associates from the inherent want of merit in the songs set, down to his name—a dire result it may be charitably assumed, of conditions under which the unhappy singer is not entirely free to do himself justice. Being however recalled on two occasions the andience were recompensed with "My Pre:ty Jane" and " Mary of Argyle " sung with a touch of the genius of that Sims Reeves who may be credited with having made these songs such lasting and deserved favourites. It is to be re- gretted that in some of Mr. Piercy's efforts there was noticable an inartistic straining to produce effect by too violent contrasts of loudly and softly rendered phrases which detracts much from the pure and sweet timbre of an excellent tenor voice. Mr. D. Ffrangeon-Davies sang "Cleansing Fires" by Virginia Gabriel with appropriate fervour and good taste. his rendering of this difficult though unostentatious song and his interpretation of the contrasted and descriptive "Tempest" (St. Quentin) proved him to be an artiste in the full sense of the word. In "The Curate's song " (The Sorcerer) and " Father o' Flynn," given in response to recalls, he gave further evidence of his versatility of style and of his power to please. Mr.Ciement Locknane played the various accompaniments in an able and intelli- gent manner, and in a pianoforte solo, :Mewed a digital skill and a refinement of expression of no mean order. A most effective and brilliant operatic quartet, in which all the vocalists were associated, brought the concert to a close. A grand pianoforte (Ernst Kaps) from Mr. Pearson's establishment. was used.

div.head: EXAMINEB, SAT UR ' 'AY, NOVEMBER 10, 1894.
div.p: THE EXAMINEB, SAT UR ' 'AY, NOVEMBER 10, 1894.
NOTES ON GAMES AlcM
ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBILL

The Cubs in the Lancashire Rugby Cup Competition had an off day on Saturdav,and indulged in " friendly" games with clubs generally supposed to be 6f a lower class to themselves. The senior clubs do not look upon these match2s very seriously now-a-days, and they generally take advantage of them to try new players,and to give the others a rest. As a result, there were some rather surprising developments, and one of these was at Lancaster where Warrington were the visitors. Lan- caster have been doing very moderately in the second division, but on Saturday they caught Warrington j minus five of their usual players, and as a result they I won easily.

It is only in accordance with the history of the past four seasons however that Warrington have suffered de- feat at this place where they appear to bounder some spell from which the' cannot free themselves. Last year they were carrying all before th,m at the time they visited Lancaster, and despite this, they had to return home defeat-d by a goal And a try to a try. The Lan- c;ister siNctators will surely before long be looking upon the home fixture with Warrington as a certain victory for them. Although Lancaster do so well at home they have always to bite the dust when they come to ‘Var- rington, so that Warrington may look forward with con- fidence to having their revenge.

Mr. Referee Underwood, who hails from Wigan. has been exceedingly fortunate since he commenced his duties of blowing the whistle. He has been " referee- ing" for two years, and has never had to do it in the rain yet. Ic appeared at one time that his good fortune had come to an'end on Saturday as the rain came down in torrents. Before the kick off, however, the sun shone out, and a glorious afternoon was the result.

The match itself was a very unsatisfactory one indeed. The firs: half was very keenly contested, and Lancaster had the lead of a try at the interval. The Warrington team quickly set to work after the resting time, and were evidently in earnest to wipe off the arrears, when an incident occurred which completely spoiled the game. The Lancaster men had temporarily invaded the War- rington quarters, when Burton secured the ball, and after a magnificent run three-quart2rs the length of the field,he successfully grounded near the posts. Following , his usual custom, after touching the ball on the ground, he left it, to escape being charged by an opponent. The ball bounced up with the force with which it was grounded, and thereupon the referee refused to award a try and only allowed a minor. The run in it2elf was worthy of a try being awarded, but Burton avers that he did touch it down, and that he did not bounce it, as the referee con- tended he had. There was a long stop after this deci- sion which was obviously most unjust, for Burton had no cause whatever to throw the ball to the ground,as he was free from all his opponents.

This incident practically settled the game, for it took all the heart out of the Warrington players, and they never looked like winning. The Lancaster players on the other hand were inspirited by this let off, and the Warrington defenders had plenty to do. Two tries were gained in the last quarter of an hour, and with the last one, from which a goal was kicked, there was a little dispute as to whether the ball had not gone over " dead ball" line.

-- I notice in the "Athletic News" that it states that Warrington played very rough, but this is unfair alto- gether. No football match is played very gently, arid the match on Saturday was neither worse nor better than an average football match is played. It is proved that Warrington did not play a rough game by the fact that there were only about two free kicks given for off side play during the afternoon. The writer of the par has evidently,drawn upon his imagination.

-- In the match, Boscow played a grand game at ful back, but the three-quarters were not fed by the halves enough. Consequently they had not much chance to shine. Burton by the run he made, showed what he can do if he has half a chance, and the players would do well if they would pass a little more to him than they have done up to the present. Clark was the best of the halves, Bate not being in his usual form. The f6rwards were very much weakened, owing to absentees, and as a result they _did not do very well against their , opponents. 4 To-day, the Warrington team engage their dear friends in Widnes. This is another plice upon which they do no shine, albeit, the games are invariably very close. The a,tmo,phere of Widnes is very depressing at any time, and the place where the football field is situated is extraordinarily depressing. It is a wonder there are no deaths from poisoning sometimes. How ever let us hope for the beat, and that Warrington Wil come out on the right side this afternoon.

_- The following is the team selented to represent War- rington in the match ar!ainst Widnes: Full back, Bos- cow ; three-quarters, Monreq, Burton, Cunningham, and Floesom ; half backs, J. T. Bate and Nevins; forwards, Turner, Bailey, Thorniley, Taylor, Savage, Buckley, Berry, and Dakin.

I notice that in the report of the Lancashire v. Cheshire match which was played at Birkenhead on Siturday, Jolley is stated to have played a grand game forward, and it is very probable thpt he will be chosen in all the remaining county matches, if not for still higher honours.

The score in the match between the Lancaster and Warrington "A "teams on Saturday, looks very much like an a3sociation football result. Three goals to nil is not often the result to record of a Rugby match, but nevertheless it speaks well for the goal-kicking abilities of the Warrington team. Several of the "A" team men had been transferred to the first team and therefore some" new blood" was brought into the " A ' team. F. Gleave was one of the players chosen for the "A " tram and he acquitted himself admirably as three- quarter back. The first half of the game was of a more even character than the second, for in the latter half cf the game Warrinmton had by far the 13.-st of the play. Lawless was in fine form at goal kicking, distinguishing himself by scoring three placed goals.

On Tuesday night, at a meeting of the Lancashire County Club held in Manchester, it was decided to pro- ceed with the charges of professionalism preferred a2alnst Tyldesley, Rochdale Hornets, Wigan,Brou hton Rangers, and Swinton. The first case taken will be the one against Wigan, and this will be heard on Tuesda.V next. The Leigh representatives attended, and applied for.a repeal of their sentence of suspension, which the committee refused to entertain.

Tee Lancashire tarn - was chosen to play against Westmoreland at Oldham nest Saturday, the only change from the team originally selected to oppose Cheshire being that Goold takes the place of Simpson in the forwards.

Those two smart junior teams, St. Mary's and Stock- ton H-ath, each did a good performance on Saturday. St. Mary's-had Lostock for their visitors, and sent them hont, defeated by six tries to nil. What was the matter with the goal kicker? He was apparently oblivious as to where the goal posts were. Stockton Heath had to tackle Standish South End on the latter's own ground, and accomplished what no other team has been able previously to do on that ground this season, by inflict- ing a defeat of a try to nil. The scorer of the try was Barber who keeps up his reputation as a prolific scorer.

A SINGULAR WILL.

Mr. oames Mack, of Edinburgh, who died last month, left a brief hologranh well written on note paper, tinder date 23rd April, 1894. The deed, which has been lodgad for registration, is as follows :—" Anything I have goes to my sister Margaret. This will is according to the moral law. As for the law of the land, I care nothing for its ignorance, thefts, and murders."

DIE PROPOSED TRANSFER OF LOCAL PARISHES.

LOCAL GOVERNMENT INQUIRY AT W ARRINGTON. At the Boa'rd-room of the Warrington Workhouse on Saturday, Mr. Jenner rust, Local Government Board inspector, Yield a public inquiry relative to the order made by the Joint Committee of the Lan- cashire and Cheshire County Councils for the trans- ference of the townships of Latchford (extra muni- cipal), Grappenh all and Thelwall from the Warring- ton Union to Runcorn Union. The Boord-room was crowded with persons interested in the matter. Mr. J. C. Sutton appeared on behalf of the Warring- ton Board of Guardians to oppose the transfer, and Mr. Bradbury, barrister, Manchester, appeared on behalf of Councillors James Fairciough, Henry Roberts, and Wm. Pierpoint, ratepayers in the townships pro- posed to be transferred, in oppPsitien to the proposal. Mr. J. L. Whittle (town clerk) appeared on behalf of the Corporation, and Mr. Moss, birrister, repsesented the Joint Committee, instructed by Mr. F. C. Hulton and Mr. R. Potts, clerks to the Lanca;hire and Cheshire County Conceits respectively. Amongst those present w:ire : Councillors James Fairclough, Henry Roberts and W. Pierpoint, Mr. W. Houghton (chairman of the War- rington Board of Guardians), Messrs. S. Davies and Geo. Pilling (vice-chairmen), and the following members : Messrs. Smith, Turton, Balharry, Warburton, Mather, A. Jolley, Mr. S. Sutton (assistant clerk,and clerk to the Rural Sanitary Authority), Mr. Shearer (relieving officer), Mr. Kerfoot (inspector), Mr. Ward (workhouse master), Mr. T. L?ngdin (borough surveyor), Dr. Gor- nail (borough medical officer), Mr. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), Mr. W. Long, Mr. Lister Kaye, Mr. Wood cock, Mr. Aldred (Grappenhall), and Mr. W. Earp C.C., The fiodlowing deputation tend() from the Runcorn Board of Guardians: —lYlessss. Mclntyre (chairman), Brandreth, Knowles, C. T. Whitley, J. M. Williams, T. Baxter, T. Handley, and John Ashton (clerk). MR. SUTTON RAISES A TECHNICAL onmenotr. At the commencement of the proceedings Mr. J. C. Sutton referred the Inspector to -article 3 of an order made under the Local Goverotnent Act stating "At least ten days before the day that any such local in- quiry (that was by the Joint Committee) is to be held a printed notice of the purport of the proposal, with the time, date, Sze., is to be be given." The notice of the : Joint Committee inquiry signed by the clerks of the County Councils simply gave them the impression that the parishes were to be considered with respect to rural sanitary administration without interfering with the Poor Law linion.—Mr.Moss here interposed,urging that no objection was taken to the notice at • the Joint Com- mittee's inquiry.—Mr. Sutton replied that he himself objectei—Mr. Moss said he was instructed that no ob- jection was =fide, and he did not see how they could go into the question of insufficiency of notice now, the whole case having been argued before the Joint Commit- tee and an order .made.—Mr. Sutton observed that he distinctly raised the question and was replied to by both Mr. Potts and Mr. Hulton. He said the question of the union as regards poor law purposes did not arise there, and both gentlemen replied that it did affect the union in that way. The Guardians had petitioned the Local Government Board about it, and if necessary they would go to the Superior Courts en the point. Then it was necessary that in the no- tice the purport of the proceedings should be given. The committee had made an order con- cerning a matter which did not appear on the notice.— Mr. Bradbury also supported the objection raised by Mr. Sutton, and stated that there was a fatal difficulty in the proceedings. Notification of the inten- tion to deal with the parishes from a poor law standpoint not having been given, he contended that the order fell to the ground.—Mr. Moss said they were not called upon to send out notices to every individual ratepayer in the district. They were sent to the overseers of the parishes concerned and to the Clerk of the Guardians, the Town Clerk of Warrington, they were duly advertised in all the Warrington papers, and some were sent by post to sun- dry parties in the unions affected. And with regard to the notice itself, paragraph six contained this clause : "Any other matter and thing which under the said Act may be necessary to. be inqUired into." The first thing that the Joint Committee were compelled by the prov- isions of the Act to inquire into was the report of the Boundary Commissioners.—The Inspector (Mr. Fust) interposed, and said they were going a little too fast. The question had been raised as to the legal validity oh the order that was being inquired into. A similar point was raised at an inquiry held at the beginning of the week at Rochdale, and he must say now, as he did then, that it was a point which he did not think himself called upon to decide. It was impossible for him to pronounce the order bad.—Mr. Sutton explained that the statement referred to by Mr. Moss' was sent by the Guardians to Mr. flulton, in response to his invitation, before notice of the inquiry was given, and the remark quoted by Mr. I‘l,)ss was appended to, and when the Guardians saw that there was no reference in the notice to a proposal for separating the parishes for poor law purposes, they supposed that the Joint Committee were influenced by that information. Proceeding, he raised objection to the validity of the order on the ground that it was not published within the ten days after the inquiry as pre- scribed by the Act, the date when it appeared being August 15th, while the inquiry was held in June. He then read the petition that has been presented by the Guardians to the Local Government Board against the order, which gave at length their reasons for not wish- ing the parishes to be transferred to Runcorn, the chief beimg the inconvenience for administrative purposes that would ‘ensue and the loss in ratable value to the Warring- ton Union.

THE EVIDENCE AGAINST THE PROPOSAL. Councillor H. ROBERTS J.P., was the first witness called and stated that he lived in Latchford without. His opinion regarding the proposed separation of Latch- ford from the Warrington Inion was that it would be a decided mistake. He spoke as a ratepayer and resident in Latchford. S 3 far as he knew the residents were opposed to the transfer. In cross-examination by Mr. Bradbury he stated that Latchford was a suburban dis- trict of Warrington at 99 per cent, of the residents had business connections with the town, and none with Run- corn. It wets within very easy access of Warrington. Referring to the lighting of the township he said they got that done by appealing to the Warrington Rural Sanitary Authority and he did not think they would have had the slightest consideration if they had had to to apply to an authority so far away and on the extreme border of the Runcorn Union. Mr. G. PILLING stated that he was a guardian for Latchford and was vice-cnairman of the Board of Guardians. Be lived in Latchford without and was chairman of the Committee which distributed, relief to that part of the Union. He spoke of the convenient situation of the Warrington Union for those who found it necessary to attend from tho parishes proposed to be transferred, and stated that he walked from Thelwall to Dutton one day that week and it took him three heurs. It would greatly inconvenience the poor people living in Latchford, Grappenhall and Thelwall if the parishes were transferred to the Runcorn Union. He also spoke of the difficulty to get near Dutton by railway. He did not think if the parishes were _transferred to Runcorn that anyone could be got to represent the townships owing to the great loss of time that would necessarily be caused in going to the meetings at Dutton.. Mr. B. SHEARER stated that he had been an officer for the Guardians for 14 years. He very frequently found that people who had been working with the farmers and others in Thelwall and Grappenhall came for relief to the Warrineton Union when sick. They would continue to do so if the townships were transferred to Runcorn. He spoke of the inconvenience to the poor people in the townships if they had to go to Dutton Workhouse for relief, school attendance fees, &c., owing to the long distance from the townships and the difficulty of getting the're. To get to the Clerk's office at Runcorn from Thelwall. the return railway fare would be 23. 7d. Councillor Jews FAIRCLOUGH stated that he resided in Latchford without. If the township was transferred to the Runcorn Union in his opinion it would be a great hardship to the inhabitants of Warrington. He did not think that the plan was workable owing to the distance from Runcorn and Dutton being SO great as compared with Warrington. Councillor W3I. PIHRPOINT stated that he resided in Grappenhall and had works in Latchford without. He thought that the geographical position of Latchford was such as to make it part cf the Borough of Warring- ton. If the Runcorn Union was allowed to absorb the township of Latchford without he thought it would act prejudicially against the Cerporation of Warrington when they applied for the extension of the Borough. He thought the transfer would be most objectionable. He attended a meeting at Grappenhall and the only reason he heard for supporting the transfer of the township to Runcorn was that they were going to save 2d. in the £. He was asked to sign a petition in favour of the transfer but he refused thinking that it might be a gain of 2d. and a lost of 4d. (Laughter). Mr. JOHN TUNSTALL stated that as assistant overseer for Latchford he had to do most of his work in that Board-room. If Latchford Without was added to the Runcorn Union there was no doubt that it would be a grew inconvenience. The residents would then have to attend before the Assessment Committee at Dutton Workhouse. Mr. ALDRED stated that he resided at Grappenhall and was an owner of property there. He objected to the transfer of the parish to Runcorn. He thought it would be a hardship on the poor people in Grappenhall, and he

was perfectly satisfied with the present arrainment. I Mr. Was. HOUGHTON said he wa,s chairman of the War- rington Board of Guardians. For many years he had resided in Thelwall and had a farm there. He thought the transfer would be most objectionable, and it would be almost impossible for the guardian to attend to his ' duties properly if he had to go to Dutton Workhouse. To take away the rateable value of the parishes from Warrington would be a great injustice. Mr. SMITH, guardian for Grappenhall, said he found it very convenient to attend to his duties at the Warring- ton Union. If the parish was put in the Runclru Union he would refuse to undertake the duties of guardian owing to tne distance ot Dutton from Grappenhall and the time he would lose. Mr. LONGDIN, borough surveyor,said that with regard to the drainage of Latchford without, the Warrington Corporation were bound to take part of it into their sewers. The district was lighted from Warrington and was supplied with water from Warrington. The inhabi- tants used the public institutions and it was really a part of Warrington. For sanitary purposes it could not be more efficiently worked. The Corporation intended to apply tO Parliament for an extension of the borough • and to ask that the ship Canal be the boundary. The inhabitants got the advantage of Warrington institu- tions' and would continue to have them, even if the small contributions paid in rates to the Warrington Guardians were taken away. If the parishes were trans- ferred to Runcorn it would be a ground of opposition to the extension of the borough. This concluded the evidence in support of the petition -.host the order. EVIDINCE IN FAVOUR OF THE ORDER. Mr. Etb._ oa, clerk to the Lancashire County Council, was called, ar, • xpiained the reason why the order had not been publishe, -itina the ten days prescribed by the , Act by the fact that t physical impossibility to • bad been 134 orders made in Lancashire carrying erovi,,ions of the Act, 103 of which were presented on one day. The Printers could not get the type set up in time. The Local Government Board had only been, able to con- firm 25 out of the 60 orders that had been sent up to them. Mr. LISTER KATE, of Grappenhall. agent for Mr J. - Chariton Parr, handed in a potition passed by the meet- ing held at Grappenhall the previous night, requestiog the Local Government Board to confirm the order. This petition, he said, was signed by 140 out of 187 inhabit- ants. Only one man had declined to sign, and they had not had time to get the others to sign. He tkkought the most sensible thing that had been proposed was to make the Ship Canal the county boundary and the boundary of Warrington. Mr. PETER WannuaToti, the guardian for Thelwall, was also called by Mr. Moss. He said he attended the meeting when a resolution was passed in fav,)ur of the transfer, and he supported the project because of the saving of 2d. in the £ which he bulievecl would be effected.—Cross-examined by Mr. Siitton, he said his house was ten miles from Dutton Workhouse, and if the transfer were made he would be unwilling to travel that distance to attend the Board meetings. Mr. Sutton, Mr. Bradbury, and Mr. Moss then addressed the Inspector in their turn on the various points raised, and the inquiry catne to a termination.
OUR LOCAL CHURCIIES-W A.RRINGTON
P.S.A. MEETING AT WYCLIFFE CHURCH.

Mr. John Porritt presided over a largely attended meeting on Sunday afternoon. He based his remarks on the text "Yet man is born unto trouble as the sparks fly upward," and referred to the value of sympathy in times of trouble. Mr. F. Smith, J.P., of Manchestsr delivered the address and spoke more particularly of the various kinds ot faces met with in the course of life. Ile also urged upon those present to strive for something noble, high and useful. Mr. Watts was the soloist for the afternoon and effectively sang the solo "Then AAA the righteous shine." The Rev. John Yonge and Mr. W. H. Wallington also took part in the meeting. SERVICES FOR THE PEOPLE.

The usual "service for the people" was held in Bold- st. Wesleyan Church on Sunday afternoon. The con- gregation was too large to be admitted into the lower portion of the building, and a considerable number of those present found it necessary to resort to the gallery, a fact which gives abundant evidence of the increasing popularity of the services. Mr. R. G. Henshall presided over the nieeting, and after the orchestral band had played a "March in G," and a hymn had been sung, Mr. Ostle read a portion of Scripture, and Mr. Summers- gill engaged in prayer. The congregation was then charmed by the excellent rendering of" Sunset" by the orchestral band. Miss Bessie Dutton gave a very ap- propriate address which was greatly appreciated by all present. A duet was effectively sung by Mrs. Bailey and Miss Brough, and a further selection of music by the band brought to a close a service which throughout was both pleasing and profitable.

HUMOROUS EVENING AT THE Y.M.C.A. A humorous and musical evening was held at the Warrington Y.M.C.A. lecture-room on Wednesday night before a very large audience. The chair was taken by Councillor J. Shaw Green who, in the course of a brief address, expressed his pleasure at seeing so favourable an audience, notwithstanding the very inclement weather. This showed, he said, the popularity of Mr. H. M. Ashton as an entertainer. He had rather an uncommon proposition to make, viz.— that it was desired that no encores should be called for owing to the length of the programme. The evening's proceedings were commenced by the chairman calling upon Mrs. H. M. Ashton and Miss E. Birtles for a piano- forte duet, entitled " Tara,ntelle." This was played with spirit and received well-merited applause. Mr. F. Fieldhouse then rendered the song "To-morrow will be Friday "in a pleasing manner. Mr. H. M. Ashton fol- lowed with the first of his selections, one from the world- famed American humorist—Mark Twain. Mr. Ashton has the knack of reading humorous bits in a humorous manner and kept his audience con- vulsr-d with merriment throughout. Mr. J. M. Bate gave an excellent rendition of "Sally in our Alley" and an interval of five minutes was then announced. The second half of the evening was initiated by "The Sunlit Highway" by Mr. Bate. Selections from Artemus Ward were then read by Mr. Ashton in a manner fully as amusing as the previous lot. Mr. F. Fieldhouse gave "To Anthea " in an admirable manner when Mr. Ash- ton was again announced to read—this time, a series of tit-bits from Max Adeler which were heartily enjoyed by his audience. The last item on the programme was a vocal duet entitled "The moon hath raised her lamp above," in the rendition of which Messrs. Bate and Fieldhouse excelled their previous performances. As no charge had been made for admission, one, as the Chair- man remarked, would be made to go out, the proceeds of which were intended to meet the expenses. At the Close of the entertainment Mr. Wyllie proposed a vote of thanks to Mr- Ashton and the other entertainers for their !kindness in appearing that evening. The motion was seconded by Dr. Bisby and carried unanimously.

div.head: ST. PETER'S CHITR6II SALE OF WORK,
div.p: ST. PETER'S CHITR6II SALE OF WORK,

A sale of work in aid of the parochial organisa- tions in connection with the St. Peter's parish, was opened on Thursday afternoon in John-8 School. The interior of the school was picturesquely decorated for the occasion by the lady members of the church. The articles on sale were of a very mis- cellaneous character, being both useful and ornamental. There were seven stalls which were placed round the sides of the room, and the following were the stall- holders :—No. 1 stall : Mrs. Savage, Miss Edgar. and Miss Bamforth ; No. 2 stall : Mrs. CuppaTe, Mrs. Place, and Misses Place ; vicarage stall : Mrs. Percival, Misses Broadbent, Mrs. Richardson, Mrs. Taylor. and Miss Smith ; men's bible stall : Mrs. Pearson, Miss Roberts, Mr. Holbrook, and Mr. Roberts : advertisement stall Mrs. Edgar, Miss Edgar, Miss Hayes, Mr. Kay, and Mr. Cowden ; refreshment stall : Misses Brookes,Miss Woods, , Miss Cuppage, Miss Smethurst, Miss Percival, Miss ' Arline Harrison, Miss Marie Randall ; flower stall : Miss Green, Miss White. There was a good attendance at the opening ceremony, which was performe Iby Mrs, Charlton Parr. Among those present were the Revs. F.W.Willis (rector), B.Percival (vicar). .T. Cooil (cnrato), Mrs. Beamont, Mrs. Carleton, Mrs. Willis, Mrs. Sharp, Mrs. Maclure (of Manchester), Mrs. Davies. Mrs. Pigot, Mrs. and Miss Reynolds, Mrs. Langham, Mr. E. Place, Mrs. Proud, Mrs. Bunch, etc. The Rev. B. PERCIVAL in opening the proceedings-said that in the first plane. he must thank Mrs. Charlton Parr for her presence that afternoon. He must also thank those who had shown their sympathy with the work in the parish, and those who had contributed to the success of the sale by sendinc, various articles and taking charge of the stalls. At the sale of work- last year they had realised £72, and from that sum, £65 had been given to the curates' fund, and the rest had gone for parochial purposes. That day they asked for £l5O, as beyond the curates' fund, they wished to extend the Sunday schools, a work that was very mueh needed. Then there was a flourishing mothers' meeting, which they wished to assist, and also a young men's club which they would like to aid. They hoped in a short time to have a boys' brigade in connection with the parish. They had been looking out for a maq to take charge of it for a long time, and he was glad to say that h. believed that they had got the right man at last. The only thing which was now required was the money. .Mr. Percival then introduced Mrs. Parr to the audience. Mrs. PARR said that she was pleased to do anything to assist the good work which was carried on in St. Peter's parish by Mr. and Mrs. Percival. They deserved every encouragement that Could be given to them, and she honed the sale would be a great success. The business of the afternoon was then commenced, and the amount realised was £
