OPENING MEETING OF A UNITED BIBLE CLASS
The opening meeting of a United Bible Clasi connected with the Sunday School Union and Y.M. C.A. was held al the rooms of the latter on Monday

evening. Mr, H. Stewart (secretary) presided, and the Rev. E. T. Reed gave an exposition of next Sun- day's lesson speaking hopefully of the class as a means of mutual help. After refreshments had been partaken of a conversation was started, _during
V,Thich the Revs. D. W. Roberts and J. Kinlan
dressed the members, tendering suitable advict-. The appointment of two secretaries brought the meeting which was well attended, to a clo4e.
ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN BAND OF HOPE. The first meeting of the St. John's Presbyterian Church Band of Hope was held in the schoolroom

of the church on Tuesday evening. A lecture,illus- trate(' by limelight views, was given by Mr. T. Longdin (borough surveyor) on a topic of great interest : "Japan, or the land of the rising sun." The lantern was manipulated in an efficient manner by Mr. H. W. Lonelin, and the chair was taken by the Rev. J. Warnock, M.A., B.D. There was a very good attendance. Moonx WESLE YA N CHOIR.

The Wesleyan Chapel choir members journeyed to Martinscroft, on Monday, where, in the Wesleyan Chapel, they rendered a service of song, entitled "Primrose Garth." The party left Moore at 2.30 p.m. by 'hus,and soon after their arrival at Martins- croft, tea was prepared for them in the chapel- room. The service, which was read by Miss B. Dutton, commenced at 7.30, the room being well filled. Solos were sung by Messrs. Birch and Antro- bus, Mrs. Birch and Miss Dolling. The anthem. "Praise the Lord, 0 my Soul," was well rendered by the Moore choir, and evidently much appre- ciated. A collection was made at the close of the service in aid of the chapel's renovation fund. SUPPOSED RELICS OF THE CIVIL WAR. in connection with the building of some shops in Sankey-st., on the site of the old circus, by Mr. Joseph Mounfield, builder, numerous excavations have been made and a few days ago the workmen' employed made an interesting discovery. At the distance of about 30 feet from the present street, they came upon traces of an old highway paved with large boulder stones, and at the limit there were traces of an old hedge-row. Behind this was found the greater part of a skeleton and beside it an old sword scabbard. It is supposed that the skeleton is the remains of a soldier hurriedly buried during the Civil War. The sword scabbard has been handed over to the Warrington Museum. Similar relics have been found in Warrington on previous occasions, especially in Battersby-lane and Church-street district. Friars Green has also been the scene of several discoveries of a like nature. _

There was a crowded attendance at the Y.M .C.A. lecture-room on Sunday afternoon, the P.S.A. for. the occasion being supplanted by a musical service to which the members of both sexes were invited,
Air. William Roberts was the chairman, and in his

address expressed his pleasure at seeing Church- men, Nonconformists of every type and a few Catholics gathered together in the room. He was also pleased that they had such a competent band as the one provided by Mr. P. Randall. The address proper was delivered by Mr. Kent, who had for the subject of an interesting address' "Music and its influence." Miss Kent rendered the solo," Gates of the West," and a violin obligato, composed by Mr. Randall was ably played Mr. J. Rigby. The pieces played by the band were ; Mozart's, " Gloria," " Diademe," and "Brazilian March." These were all executed in good style by the instrumentalists. Mr. P. Randall was the conductor.

div.head: COMING OF AGE OF CANON PENRHYN'S SON.
div.p: COMING OF AGE OF CANON PENRHYN'S SON.

On Monday, Mr. Charles Penrhyn, only son of the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, rector and rural dean of Win wick, came of age. In celebration of the happy event the flag on the Parish Church was hoisted, and the hells were chimed at intervals during the day and evening. In the evening a huge bonfire was lighted and a fine display of fireworks t)ok place at the Rectory in honour of the event, and also in celebration of it being the Gunpowder Plot. There was a large attendance including the school children. During the evening, the Win- wick Glee Club sang a number of glees, songs, &c., at the Rectory in a highly efficient manner, for which they were complimented. ,Mr. Charles Pen- rhyn has received several valuable and useful pres- ents, as well as the well wishes of a large circle of friends and the inhabitants of Winwick generally. CHURCH LAD'S BRIGADE: UNITED CHURCH PARADE. A United Church Parade, of the Padgate and Warrington St. Elphin's companies of the Church Lads' Brigade took place at Padgate on Sunday atternoon. The Padgate company was marched to near the Warrington Cemetery where they met the St. Elphin's company. There a procession was formed, a detachment of the Warrington Volunteer Band, under the direction of Bandmaster T. Arm- strong, taking the lead, followed by the Padgate Church Lad's Brigade Bugle Band, and the two companies bringing up the rear. The Padgate com- pany was in command of Captain F. M. Appleton, who was accompanied by Lieutenants Black well an Granger: whilst Captain J. D. Buckton was in charge of St. Elphin's, together with Lieutenants Sherwood and Willis. Scores of people lined the road from the Cemetery to Padgate. The two bands played alternately whilst proceeding to the church The church was crowded, a great number being unable to obtain accommodation. The service was of a special character, and was conducted by the chaplain, who also preached the sermon. The offer- tory was in aid of the funds of the Padgate Church Lad's Brigade, and realised a good sum. After the service the lads were put, through several move- ments, and afterwards marched to their respective headquarters. The parade was a success in every respect.. THE FATALITY AT MESSRS. WALKER'S BREWERY. An inquest was held in the Parade Room on Monday touching the death of John Granger who died at tne Warrington Infirmary on Friday after- noon through being scalded in a vat at Messrs. Walker's Brewery, Dellam-lane. Mr. S. Brighouse was the coroner, Mr. H. Greenall, solicitor, repre- sented Messrs. Walker's and Mr. Newlands, factory inspector, was also present. The first witness called was Jane Granger, who stated that the de- ceased was her husband. She saw him at the In- firmary on Thursday evening,and was present when he died on f riday afternoon. Tre did not, tell her how the accident happened. He had been working at the brewery eight or nine years and was well acquainted with the work.—Samuel Warburton stated that he was a labourer at the brewery, and knew deceased. The accident happened at about six o'clock on Thursday evening. The deceased was emptying a hot vat. Ile saw him get on the edge of the vat in order to tighten the strap to make it work the pulley. The strap was slipping round the pulley and not working satisfactorily. To make it tighter deceased pressed one hand on the strap. Witness was working at, the next vat. He heard deceased scream, but when witness got there the deceased had scrambled out of the vat. He was then taken to the Infirmary. Witness had got on the vat to tighten the strap in the same way as de- ceased hut if the foreman had seen him do it he would have complained about it. When the strap did not act the hops had to be carried out by the man. The belt which worked the pulley was what they called a ring belt, and one of them had broken. In answer to the factory Inspector witness said that the lever to start the pulley was about six yards from where the accident took place. They had been warned about getting on the vat, and pressing on the strap.—Michael Hoy said he was foreman under-brewer, and the de- ceased had no right to stand on the vat. He saw the deceas^d get up and said "Granger get off that vat, how many more times am I to warn you." Deceased replied " I will be all right.' He was walking along when he heard screams and saw deceased getting out of the vat—Mr. Samuel Pnr,nns emnloved at the brewery also stater that he '.rt.-1 warned deceased about standing on the vat. Deceased had no right to touch the strap. Inspec- tor Newlands said he had inspected the pl9ce of the accident and so far as the Act of Parliament was concerned it had been complied with. The jury re- turned a verdict of " Accidental Death " and sug- gested that Messrs. Walker should put up a printed notice to warn workmen of the danger of standing on the vat.

div.head: TEA MEETING AND CONCERT.
div.p: TEA MEETING AND CONCERT.

On Friday evening a public tea meeting was held in the Church Institute, Moore, when nearly two hundred were entertained, the room being filled to its utmost limits. After tea Captain Widdrington, of Moore Hall, presided at the concert. Previous to the commencement of the programme the Rev. T. Whitley, vicar of Daresbury, as president of the Institute, spoke of the great loss to the institution, and indeed the whole parish, had recently sustained in the removal from amongst them of the late Canon Heron, the donor and founder of the Institute. Captain Widdrington made a few remarks and promised on behalf of Mrs. Widdrington to provide extra accommodation. An excellent programme was then proceeded with, consisting of songs, recitations' duets, and violin solos, in which the following ladies and gentlemen ably took part : Miss Wakefield, Miss Whieldon, Misses Litton Misses Oxley, Misses Lawless and :Lambert, Messrs. P. Lawless, Scattergood, Warburton, P. Owen, L. Foster, J. Foster, and J. Wright. A special feature of the concert was the violin solos so well rendered by Miss Whieldon. The accompaniments were also played by Miss Wakefield. The Pww. T. Whitley proposed a vote of thanks to the entertainers. The motion was seconded and heartily agreed to, and the proceed- ings were brought to a conclusion. . _

div.head: WYCLIFEE YOUNG PEOPLE'S SOCIETY.
div.p: WYCLIFEE YOUNG PEOPLE'S SOCIETY.

The usual weekly meeting of this society on onday evening was presided over by Mr. T. Haw- thorn. There was a good attendance. The Rev. J. Yonge delivered an admirable lecture on " Oliver Wendell Holmes." The lecturer at the outset of his lecture spoke of the value of studi ig the biogra- phies of great men and the inspiring influence they had upon the mind. Referring to the year 1800 the date of birth of Dr. Oliver Wendell Holmes he stated that it also witnessed the birth of at least four other illustrious people, viz. Tennyson, Gladstone, Mrs. Browning and Edgar Allen Poe. The lecturer proceeded to give a brief sketch of Dr. Holmes' career. He was the son of a Congregational minister but he connec..ed himself with the Unitarian body. The lecturer's opinion was that Dr. Holmes adopted that faith owing to the hyper- Calvanistic doctrine which permeated early Con- gregationalism in America. It was not until 1885 that Dr. Holmes resigned his professorship in the Harvard Medical College. Toe humour in Dr. Holmes' writing, unlike most American humour,was refined. At intervals the rev, gentleman read in excellent style several of Dr. Holmes' poems,includ- ing " My Aunt," " The Comet," "Sweet Little Man," and the ballad "The spectre pig." Extracts from the Breakfast Table series of essays and several hymns, including the last from the late Dr's. per., " 0 Love Divine," were also read. A discussion afterwards ensued in which the tollowing took part : rhe Chairman, -Messrs. R. Wyllie, W..Bes- wick, W. H. Payton, S. Rowlands, and T.
